The order matters: if you treat open models purely as a cost-cutting measure, you will misjudge why they are spreading so fast inside the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption onto open models, currently mostly US and European ones, while also evaluating Chinese models.

4:05 Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw
The per-user token usage curve on Ollama's cloud has two clear inflection points. The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM and MiniMax launched in succession, and for the first time open models could carry a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, support, marketing and sales can all hand a hard problem to an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and pulling data along the way, burning enormous numbers of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million is the technical precondition for this surge.

8:08 Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill
Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors ahead of launch, but Jeff says getting a model weeks early counts as lucky; most of the work is crammed into the final 24 hours before release. Three things have to land at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, to make sure it is fast, accurate and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are plenty of open-source harnesses now, like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the biggest growth day. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, the inference layer and the application runtime all have to be glued together, and it is a combinatorial explosion problem.

14:11 Above the token is where the new scarcity lives
Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (wiring company data and context into the model), coordination (a single request spawns a pile of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, that need scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgement: tokens are already in oversupply, dozens of open model providers can supply them, and what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B on top of those tokens. Following the path of cloud computing, developers will ultimately prefer the best standalone product at every layer rather than something bundled together like Heroku or Google App Engine.

17:14 Stateful things will not sink into the model layer
Asked whether harnesses will be absorbed by the model, Jeff's judgement is that the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but a few categories cannot. One is state — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up with the latest data, so storage is a huge standalone problem space. The other is credential management and security. Open models do not come with a whole security toolchain the way closed providers do, and that is critical to enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

18:15 Eighty percent of tokens go open, but only twenty percent of budget
Jeff's steady-state judgement: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will go through open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget flows to open source. The open community is driving costs extremely low, so maybe only 10% to 20% of spend lands on open models. The hardest work stays with the frontier labs, because that is where the best researchers are; the big middle is open and closed combined. He uses a law firm as the analogy: the partner hands work down to a pile of associates.

22:19 Local and cloud model mixes are not the same thing at all
On local models, US and Chinese models are roughly neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a three-way mix of US, European and Chinese, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of use cases is clear too: coding agents write code and tests, hit many hard problems, and mostly rely on large cloud models; end-to-end low-difficulty workflows like document processing run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, plus a router deciding when to go up to a large model.

29:25 The Flash tier is the precondition for unlimited tokens
Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, less than 3 months behind the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve was extreme efficiency. For models like DeepSeek Flash, the key metric is not just low cost per token but low cost per task. These models are good enough for 80% of tasks, fast and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually get back to that state, but it requires model architectures trained specifically for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is precisely the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.

item.title: One Report Closed Over a Hundred Medical Schools, and Black Doctors Were Cut Off for a Generation
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: The Flexner Report is usually written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years afterward no new Black medical school appeared.
item.content:encoded:
The Flexner Report is usually written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years afterward no new Black medical school appeared.

Medium information density. The first half is a chronological slog through Flexner's life; the real value is in the second half, on how the report reshaped medical education and how it cut off the supply of Black doctors.

6:09 The report's author was not a doctor but an education reformer
Abraham Flexner was not a medical man. In 1890 he ran an experimental school with no fixed curriculum, no exams and no grades, and its students still got into good schools; in 1908 he wrote The American College, A Criticism, attacking American higher education, which is why Henry Smith Pritchett of the Carnegie Foundation came to him and asked him to turn the same critical eye on the medical schools of the United States and Canada. He spent two years travelling to 155 medical schools, recording admissions requirements, faculty, finances, laboratories and hospital affiliations school by school, and in 1910 delivered Medical Education in the United States and Canada. It was precisely because he was an outsider rather than a member of the medical community that the assessment dared to be so unsparing.

14:23 Medical schools were still teaching out-of-date knowledge
In the fifty years before the report, bacteriology, diagnostic technique and surgery were all changing fast, but medical schools had no common standards. At many schools the faculty were practising physicians who taught the way they themselves had been taught and did not update the content. The result was that the care the doctors they produced gave their patients was, at best, antiquated and, at worst, life-threatening. Admissions standards were just as chaotic: when the report was published, 74% of medical schools required only a high school diploma, some accepted even a high school equivalency certificate, only one in five required more than two years of college coursework, and many schools were essentially for-profit businesses.

18:31 He recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools
Flexner set standards first and then graded school by school: admission should require college-level biology, chemistry and physics; the curriculum should include classroom and laboratory work in anatomy, pathology, bacteriology and pharmacology; there should be a teaching hospital for hands-on practice; and teachers should be salaried, full-time teaching and research staff rather than physicians practising on the side. He published the results by state and by school, naming dirty laboratories and lax standards, and criticising course schedules that left students sitting for hours, exhausted, listening to dull lectures by part-time instructors. In the end he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools. Within ten years the number of American medical schools was down to half, the surviving schools reformed their standards and curricula, and laboratory and clinical teaching were modernised on a large scale. In Canada only one school made the closure recommendation list, and in the end it did not close.

23:43 He never did the books on Black medical schools
The report was equally unsparing toward Black medical schools, writing that five of the seven "can make no valuable contribution at this moment", and affirming only Howard and Meharry as worth developing. But the assessment did not take into account that Black medical schools charged far lower tuition than white schools, had smaller endowments, and were already running on extremely thin margins. He wrote that "the Negro needs good schools rather than many schools", and said that one of the most important duties of Black doctors and Black nurses was to teach hygiene rather than life-saving skills — a statement that is itself racist. Every Black medical school he named as inadequate closed: the first four closed before 1914, the fifth in 1915, and the last held on until 1923.

25:48 The next Black medical school had to wait until 1966
Howard and Meharry survived and are still there today. But the next medical school aimed primarily at Black students was Charles R. Drew Medical School in Los Angeles, which did not open until 1966, and then in response to the health-access needs of the Black community; the one after that was Morehouse School of Medicine in Atlanta in 1975. The direct consequence of narrowing the options was a huge care gap: many potential doctors were shut out of educational opportunity by geography, and Black patients were often cared for by white doctors who, even at best, carried built-in racial bias. An expert panel convened by the AMA's Institute for Ethics in 2005 concluded that Flexner's "good schools rather than many schools" ensured that medicine remained segregated, and that the communities that most needed doctors were the ones left without them.

26:51 The AMA was paying behind Carnegie's project
One fact not disclosed at the time: the Carnegie Foundation hired Flexner for this project, and the AMA was also a sponsor. There is also an unresolved question — whether someone connected to the AMA accompanied him on some of the school visits. He said different things at different times, sometimes that the person went with him, later that they merely met there, so whether the report was subject to more direct directional influence cannot be determined to this day.

28:53 Did he know he was constraining Black medicine?
He knew. The report contains a passage of idealistic colouring, saying that building up Howard and Meharry would benefit the nation far more than barely sustaining more schools. In 1933 he wrote to the board of the institute he had founded, arguing that hiring and admissions must "not directly or indirectly consider race, religion or sex". One explanation comes from his biographer Thomas Neville Bonner: when Flexner was growing up in Louisville, the local Black community had more services and opportunities than in many places, with a dozen or so Black schools and vocational training in medicine and law for Black students; the Flexners were not well off, there were Black families among the neighbours, and he and his siblings often played with Black children in the community. This may have left him overly idealistic about the reality of Black family life, and he later admitted that it was not until he began studying educational institutions that he realised how disadvantaged those Black classmates of his had been.

35:01 The hygiene line may not have been his own
The claim that hygiene was the main duty of Black doctors is one of the key pieces of evidence for calling Flexner racist. But the leaders of Meharry and Howard had said similar things in 1907 and 1908 — two or three years before the report — and those leaders were white too. This suggests Flexner's formulation may have been a restatement of the schools' established mission rather than a judgement he arrived at independently. In 2011 Lynn E. Miller and Richard M. Weiss, writing in the Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences, proposed another possibility: that this language was in fact opening up a public health role for the doctors at these schools, in order to win support across the racial divide — because those statements about hygiene being the most urgent need were immediately followed by the conclusion that these institutions obviously ought to be supported. In 2008 the AMA issued a public apology for its history of racial inequality.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Nested Loops, but a Loop Only Climbs to a Local Optimum
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
item.description: After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. A loop will climb you to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.
item.content:encoded:
After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. A loop will climb you to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.

Anish strings together agent deployment, model pricing and the consumer AI bottleneck into one line, and the second half — on moats and product problems — is worth more than the first.

0:00 Ideas that are too small get no funding now
Anish says that three years ago, if a company wanted to do something too grand, a16z would pass; today it is the reverse — ideas that are too small, too local, they do not want to touch. The reason is that model capability has torn down the ‘can it be done’ threshold, and the remaining constraint is ambition itself. He calls this technology ‘unbundling skill from desire’: not only can productivity be amplified, the scale of what you want to do can be amplified too.

6:10 It is not recursive self-improvement, it is autocatalytic
Anish pushes back on the ‘fast takeoff’ narrative: the people who understand it best in the labs do not say RSI (recursive self-improvement), they say autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own process, but not truly recursively. He gives two counterexamples: first, economic diffusion is extremely slow, and when he went back to his hometown he found people's lives had barely changed; second, many problems are simply not intelligence bound — give FedEx or Domino's a data center full of PhDs and it still will not make supply chains and pizza exponentially crush everything.

8:16 Using AI and reorganising around AI are two different things
Anish uses the diffusion of electricity as an analogy: from the invention of electricity to factories actually reorganising took 40 years, and it meant burning down the old plants and rebuilding, not swapping coal for electricity. Today the most aggressive companies redesign everything around models, while slower companies just grant permissions to existing roles and functions. He also cites the Mexican used-car company Kavak's Jedi Academy: a six-week course teaching everyone including mechanics to use the new tools, and at graduation each person delivers an agent in the production environment.

11:18 Companies will become a series of nested loops
Anish's steel man: after prompt comes agent (a loop of model plus tools, memory, skill files), after agent comes loop (a group of agents doing a task). Coding got there first because the models are best, the users are the most technical, and a mature loop already existed — bug report comes in, generate a reproduction, fix it, high-risk changes get human confirmation, low-risk ones ship directly, and it can even automatically reply to the customer. Above that there is loop per person, loop per job function, loops across business units, up to a loop that can run most of the company.

14:18 A loop only climbs to a local optimum and stops
The growth team's version of a loop: each variant is generated automatically, measured automatically, and once it reaches statistical significance it converges and ships, with a long-term holdout left in place, and then the next experiment begins. But Anish stresses that a loop will hit a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need out of distribution thinking and human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain. His example is telling Claude ‘make me a million dollars, no mistakes allowed’ — it cannot do it, because the direction has to be set by a human.

21:32 Frontier model pricing is actually irrational
Anish explains model choice with Pareto efficiency: frontier models are ‘irrationally priced’ on the price-performance curve — one more IQ point might cost 100 times more than Opus. But for industries with unbounded upside like drug discovery, that one extra IQ point might be worth a trillion-dollar outcome, so paying that price is rational; for work with bounded upside like law and finance, you just want Pareto efficiency and a cheap, good-enough open-weight model. The conclusion is that the two architectures will coexist, not one or the other.

31:46 People want to spend time, not save it
Anish says ‘loop, make me happier’ is the big opportunity: people say they want to be more efficient, but actually they want to spend time — the world's biggest products are entertainment and social, not productivity tools. He distinguishes two kinds of users: the AI users on X fear falling into a permanent underclass and argue endlessly about whether GLM or Kimi is stronger; the Instagram user just thinks ‘this is a better Google search’. He thinks this is not a model or capability problem, it is a product design problem: for the past 40 years we built technology that extends the intellect, and we did not build things that extend the soul.

34:49 Consumer AI is still stuck in iPhone 2010
Anish compares now to iPhone 2010 — Airbnb, WhatsApp, Uber had not appeared yet. Three things are holding consumer back: models are too expensive, so free products are hard; the interface problem, chat only suits ‘the highest agency people in the world’ like Elon and Sam, while the ideal interface for ordinary consumers is TikTok, and you need to find something between chat and TikTok; and the technology has been too skewed toward productivity rather than human connection and entertainment. He thinks all three are now loosening: open-weight models have brought costs down sharply, founders like Eugenia are seriously thinking about interfaces, and Brian Chesky has also set up a lab focused on the next generation of interfaces.

item.title: Copper grades have fallen from 2% to 0.4%, while AI's power demand is going to the moon
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.description: Global copper grades keep sliding and new mines take 35 years to permit, while an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.
item.content:encoded:
Global copper grades keep sliding and new mines take 35 years to permit, while an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.

Robert Friedland lays out copper's supply-demand deadlock with 40 years of mining experience: falling grades, 8-year equipment lead times, sulfuric acid shortages. High information density, but the real goods only come in the second half.

14:30 The next 18 years must dig up all the copper of the past 10,000
Friedland offers an arithmetic that makes you squirm: humanity has mined 700 million metric tons of copper in all of history, and to recover all of it you would have to dismantle the US and Europe back to the mammoth age to get roughly 700 million tons back. But at the current pace of the global economy, just sustaining 3% GDP growth — not even counting EVs and data centers — means the next 18 years must dig up the same amount of copper as the past 10,000 years. And people in the industry broadly think that's impossible, because the US has deindustrialized and hasn't built a single copper smelter or nuclear plant since.

22:51 The world's largest copper mine's grade is in free fall
Friedland dissects Escondida: when this, the world's largest copper mine, was discovered a generation ago, its grade was close to 2%; today it's down to 0.8%, and within two years it will fall to 0.4%. Falling grades mean crushing and grinding more rock to extract less metal, and crushing and grinding account for 4% to 5% of global energy consumption. The mine sits at 12,000 feet in the Andes, in the Atacama Desert where it hasn't rained in 30,000 years, and it takes two cubic meters of water to crush one cubic meter of rock. They built a $4 billion desalination plant and spend $1 million a day on electricity pumping water from sea level up to 12,000 feet. The upshot: just keeping this one mine producing requires another $10 to $12 billion of investment.

27:54 An AI search uses 30x the power of a normal search
Friedland gives a concrete energy comparison: one Google search consumes the electricity to light a 100-watt bulb for 12 seconds, while one AI search — he uses ChatGPT4 and Cloud — uses 30x that, equivalent to lighting a 100-watt bulb for two or three minutes. Every five-year-old in the world with an iPad is using AI search, and power demand ‘literally goes to infinity’. He also points out: nothing about the internet is inherently green, and this studio itself is copper-intensive and energy-intensive.

34:01 Sulfuric acid prices rose more than sixfold in eight months
About 25% of the world's copper needs sulfuric acid for leaching and extraction, and sulfuric acid comes mainly from Middle Eastern natural gas. After the Strait of Hormuz closed, sulfuric acid prices went from $150 a ton to over $1,000 a ton in eight months. Russia and China have already banned sulfuric acid exports. Friedland's company benefits, because it built Africa's largest copper smelter where sulfuric acid is a byproduct — they sell the acid to fellow copper miners in Congo, at ever higher prices. But he warns: without more sulfuric acid, global food prices will rise too, because sulfuric acid is also used to make fertilizer.

51:25 Buying one large motor means waiting eight years
Friedland tells a supply-chain story absurd in its specificity: building the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine in Mongolia's Gobi, they needed large motors about 40 feet in diameter, and just the ring gear took four and a half years to arrive. Today the same equipment takes eight to ten years, ‘if ever’. And hyperscalers wanting gas turbines face lead times of six to eight years. An even more extreme example: a Congo copper mine flooded by an earthquake needed pumps to drain it, pumps moving 1,300 liters per second with a head three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. They called the US and Germany, and neither could build them, because they couldn't get samarium-cobalt magnets. Only China could build them within 30 days. At the time, the flooding was costing $15 million a day in lost revenue.

58:35 US miners earn $100 an hour; Congo engineers earn $800 a month
Friedland directly compares cost structures: Congo copper grades run 3% to 6%, the median age is 18.7, and a Congo software engineer who knows AI earns $800 to $1,000 a month. Mining copper in the US, by contrast, means the United Steelworkers demand over $100 an hour for underground work, plus environmental legislation and legal constraints, making costs far higher. He also criticizes the net present value model invented by the financial system: it was designed for oil and gas, but mines can't be shoehorned into it — an oil field decays fast if you don't invest, whereas a mine with 100 years of reserves won't deplete like an oil field. The NPV model suppresses mining company valuations, and today mining companies' total market cap is under 1% of the S&P 500, the lowest in history.

1:02:39 Tariffs could keep US copper mines alive, but they'd stoke inflation
Asked about copper tariffs, Friedland says explicitly he won't take a position, but he can argue both sides: if copper is $6 and you add a 30% tariff, that's $1.80, taking copper to $7.80, and he could afford American miners' wages, making mining in the US feasible. But the other side is domestic inflation, possibly higher rates, and with midterms coming, it's a political question. He boils it down to: do you actually want to reindustrialize America? If you can't even build nuclear plants and ships, you lose sovereignty. Last year the US built about 8 ships; China built 1,000.

1:04:42 Governments are quietly stockpiling copper, and no one can tally supply and demand
Friedland raises an overlooked phenomenon: governments are buying copper as a proxy for money, and not reporting it. He says no one can calculate the supply-demand balance for any metal, because ‘why would you’. Meanwhile China is buying gold and selling US Treasuries, and a great debasement trade is beginning. Hedge funds borrow yen and depend on yen weakness so they never have to repay. He thinks we're at an inflection point, where everything is becoming naked and globally scrutinizable.

item.title: A US measles death is erased from CDC data, and state reporting becomes negotiable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/
item.description: The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent matters more than the case: state reporting has become something to negotiate.
item.content:encoded:
The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent matters more than the case: state reporting has become something to negotiate.

A clinical-update show: the first stretch is a pandemic data rundown, and the two densest segments are the measles death dispute in the middle and the COVID vaccine cardiovascular benefit later.

4:06 Florida now has locally acquired dengue
Griffin says he no longer needs to leave the country to see dengue cases: in the past week alone Florida had 32 locally acquired infections, more than 70 locally acquired dengue cases cumulatively, and 14 virus-positive mosquito pools detected across 5 counties. In the same segment he notes a CDC health advisory issued that day — rabies-related consultations since July 2026 are up 17% over the same period in 2025, including mass exposure events, against a backdrop of US pet owners hesitating to vaccinate animals against rabies. Put together, these two things show not an isolated event with some pathogen but that the US has abandoned lines of defense against preventable diseases it mastered decades ago.

6:09 NIH money is being moved to the Department of Defense
Nature reported that NIH is seeking to transfer hundreds of millions of dollars of research projects from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to the Department of Defense (referred to in the piece as the Department of War) biodefense program, and two NIH employees told Nature the two sides had signed a preliminary agreement. The Department of Defense responded confirming a research agreement had been signed, allowing "project-by-project strategic collaboration," and said "any suggestion that this agreement was reached in secret is false" — but the response never mentions the money. Griffin's follow-up is direct: biodefense itself is fine, the Department of Defense has plenty of money, it does not need to reach into the pockets of an already underfunded NIH.

9:09 HPV vaccination has not budged in four years, stuck at 77.7%
The MMWR adolescent vaccination coverage survey shows HPV vaccine coverage among 13- to 17-year-olds has not risen since 2021, now stalled for a fourth consecutive year: in 2025 only 77.7% had received at least one dose and only 63.4% completed the series. By comparison, Tdap and meningococcal vaccines have held at about 90% since 2019, with far smaller geographic variation than HPV. The HPV vaccination gap between rural and urban areas exists at every poverty level, whereas the meningococcal rural-urban gap appears only among adolescents below the poverty line. Griffin's comment: this vaccine can 100% prevent cervical, anogenital and head and neck cancers — why aren't we doing it.

15:15 Congo Ebola: only 15% of new cases come from known contacts
MMWR used a set of "operational indicators" to assess control of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo over the 21 days from July 31 to August 21: the average proportion of alerts investigated within 24 hours was 83%, against a target above 90%; an average of only 10.6 contacts were identified per confirmed case, against a target above 20; only 15% to 20% of newly confirmed cases had previously been identified as known contacts, against a target above 90%, meaning most cases are occurring outside known chains of transmission; and 59% of Ebola deaths occurred outside Ebola treatment centers, when that number should be zero. Griffin's conclusion is that the outbreak is far from controlled, with 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths cumulatively.

17:16 The CDC dropped a state-reported measles death from its tally
On August 25 the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-related deaths in Lancaster County, the state's first in 35 years; the next day RFK Jr. suggested on X that the deaths might have been fabricated by the governor's staff. Late on Sunday night, August 30, the CDC published its weekly measles update, replacing the two deaths with an asterisk and saying available information could not determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths. According to The Washington Post and CNN, the decision came from new CDC director Erica Schwarz, at RFK Jr.'s direction. Vincent points out the key fact: state and local health departments do the case investigation, apply the case definition and report to the CDC; the CDC has no independent investigative authority and historically only receives and aggregates, checking later. This time the CDC was itself embedded in the Pennsylvania investigation, so the "insufficient information" claim does not hold up.

19:18 Nobody routinely screens the dead for measles
A SIDRAP commentary dismantles the "measles wasn't the direct cause of death" line: clinically there is no admission swab, no routine testing before delivery or surgery, and no laboratory reason to go looking for measles virus in someone without symptoms; CDC guidance for clinicians is to look first at clinical features — fever, cough, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, rash — and only then consider testing. So when measles turns up positive in a death investigation, it is usually because there was already a clinical or epidemiological reason to test. The piece concedes the probability of an unrelated death coinciding with an unrelated measles infection is not zero, but small enough that a rational person should shift their judgment substantially. In the Pennsylvania case specifically: the mother also became severely ill after another child was infected with measles, delivered about a month early, and the infant was born not breathing and could not be resuscitated; measles virus was detected in the infant's lung tissue.

22:20 The structure of the death certificate is being used as a shield
Much of the dispute stems from how death certificates are structured, something most people have never had reason to learn. Part I lists the causal chain leading to death, with the top line the immediate cause and the lines below it the conditions that produced it, ending with the underlying cause that started the whole sequence; Part II, per the National Center for Health Statistics handbook, is "other significant conditions contributing to death." So the immediate cause line reads pneumonia, encephalitis, or in this case splenic rupture, while measles appears in Part II — measles caused the splenic rupture, and the splenic rupture killed the child. Treating "the immediate cause wasn't measles" as evidence that measles was irrelevant mistakes the structure of a form for a medical conclusion.

24:20 The real damage is the precedent, not these two cases
Vincent lays out the consequence clearly: if the CDC can refuse to accept a state's statutory report until it is satisfied, then the national count becomes negotiable and every state's data is subject to federal review under undisclosed standards. Former CDC medical examiner Deb Hury told STAT that states have always reported deaths and the CDC has always counted them. Pennsylvania also pushed back on the federal account of "what information was actually provided," saying both deaths were reported to the CDC's measles response team, that the state epidemiologist conducted a thorough investigation, and that per the Pennsylvania health commissioner the CDC was in fact embedded in that investigation. Griffin adds: whichever team is in power now, someday the other team will be, and the federal government should not be touching the data.

item.title: Active management giant moves HQ to Nashville, saves $85 million a year
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-mastersinbiz-主动管理巨头把总部搬去纳什维尔-一年省下8500万美元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-mastersinbiz-主动管理巨头把总部搬去纳什维尔-一年省下8500万美元/
item.description: Alliance Bernstein moved from New York to Nashville, saving about $85 million a year, and didn't force any portfolio manager to relocate — the savings are real estate and people costs, the bet is on hiring people New York can't.
item.content:encoded:
Alliance Bernstein moved from New York to Nashville, saving about $85 million a year, and didn't force any portfolio manager to relocate — the savings are real estate and people costs, the bet is on hiring people New York can't.

A 32-year JPMorgan veteran explains the structural shifts in asset management: active to passive, ETFs replacing mutual funds, private credit entering 401(k)s. Medium information density; the second half is worth more than the first.

9:18 When active management gets squeezed by passive, cut costs before talking growth
When Bernstein took over, Alliance Bernstein was hitting the biggest industry headwind since the financial crisis: money moving from active to passive, fees compressing across the board, institutional sales commissions falling from 20 to 25 cents per share all the way to a few cents or less than a cent. The firm itself had just been through a collapse — the merged AUM had touched nearly $900 billion mid-quarter, and by 2012 was down to $380 billion; in 2006 about 70% was equity assets, by 2012 only 30%. His predecessor, brought in from Goldman Sachs, restructured, replaced some teams, and equity performance began to recover, which is what got the firm back to net inflows. Bernstein says what he brought was not firefighting but a more global perspective and a focus on distribution.

21:39 Moving to Nashville saves $85 million a year, and no one is forced to move
The firm was debating whether it could still afford a New York headquarters, and ultimately chose Nashville from five candidate cities — the reason being ‘wanting to be a big fish in a small pond’, which couldn't be done in Charlotte or Dallas. The move saves about $85 million a year, part real estate, part people. The key design: no portfolio manager is forced to relocate, because the firm is a ‘price taker’ for that kind of talent. As a result, nearly 100 portfolio managers chose to move. The challenges are concrete: Nashville is the capital of healthcare services, and it's hard to find international tax accountants and technology and operations people with traditional Wall Street training locally; but the firm received a flood of resumes from Atlanta, Chicago, New York, Boston and the West Coast.

25:44 Sell-side research without cross-subsidy can only be a joint venture
Bernstein says a buy-side firm owning a sell-side research business is a historical accident. Almost every peer uses equity capital markets or prime brokerage to cross-subsidize research, and Alliance Bernstein had none of those businesses to subsidize with. So they put the research business into a joint venture with Société Générale, and made clear it would eventually transition fully to SocGen. He specifically mentions the other side's concern was culture — a large French institution facing a group of Americans and Brits — so it had to be done step by step, very carefully. The transition period is five years from the JV anniversary, and they are still midway through it.

37:08 Banks are inherently unsuited to holding long-duration fixed-rate assets
Bernstein uses his experience in leveraged finance at JPMorgan to explain the structural opportunity in private credit: banks are highly leveraged players operating with short-term funding, inherently unsuited to holding long-duration, especially fixed-rate, assets. JPMorgan at the time spent a lot of time and money trying to securitize its loan book, and credit derivatives started there. Insurance companies and funds are better homes for these assets, because funds don't offer true liquidity options and therefore have no run risk. He states plainly that in credit there is no maturity transformation, and apart from interest and principal payments there should never be any liquidity.

40:14 Private credit's problem isn't defaults, it's insufficient disclosure
Asked how the industry gets past the first-half difficulties this year, Bernstein's answer is education and transparency: tell clients how many names are on the watch list, how many have stopped accruing interest. He says there is currently no mandatory disclosure requirement, but regular updates to clients make them more comfortable, and one should ‘over-communicate in times like these’. He also characterizes the problem as structural rather than systemic: defaults are a normal part of lending, and models typically already build in 2%, 3%, 4% default expectations; the problem was a handful of companies, plus fraud has always existed; what really went wrong was structure and pricing getting out of balance for a while. His conclusion is that after this experience, now is actually a better entry point.

43:14 Private credit in 401(k)s: fees are not the obstacle
Bernstein thinks target-date funds and 401(k)s may be exactly the right place for private credit: demand is highly predictable, professional managers make the decisions, and plan sponsors are themselves sophisticated investors. Alliance Bernstein worked with Brookfield and Carlisle to develop vehicles that can be used alongside target-date funds, building diversified exposure to private credit, private equity and private real estate. He admits the industry has been too optimistic about the pace of adoption, that plan sponsors are conservative, and that this will take many years, but in a decade it will probably be part of large plans. On the fee objection, his response: these are institutional buyers who will drive a hard bargain; and private assets are only a small part of the target-date portfolio, so the impact on total fees is limited.

47:18 Retirement planning should go through retirement, not stop at retirement
Bernstein points to Australia's superannuation funds as an example, saying they are thought leaders on how to think about retirement, and one key practice is designing the glide path to go through retirement rather than stop at retirement. His reasoning: what most people need least at 65 is to hold mostly short-term fixed income and cash, because they may have another 20 to 25 years to live. More practically, many people don't have enough money to retire, will delay retirement and look for supplemental income. He also proposes a specific mechanism: rather than buying an annuity all at once at retirement, design the target-date fund to leave a pool of liquidity at age 75 to buy an annuity, which can significantly lower the cost of the annuity while extending income security over a longer lifespan.

51:26 AB is the last publicly traded partnership
Bernstein says AB is probably the last publicly traded partnership, a structure rare outside energy MLPs. It means issuing K-1 tax forms, and institutions have an allergic reaction to K-1s, which limits institutional ownership. He describes the stock as ‘a bond with an equity option’, essentially high-yield debt plus an equity kicker. Asked why not change the structure to make the stock pop, his answer is direct: if they changed the structure and the stock didn't pop, a lot of people would be unhappy; and most shareholders would be negatively affected on taxes, so the board has to consider it, but the honest answer is there's no certainty.

item.title: The Oldest Manuscript of The Song of Roland Is Actually an English Performance Copy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
item.description: The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by the degree of dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.
item.content:encoded:
The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by the degree of dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.

This is a members-only sample episode, medium information density, but it gets very concrete about how a manuscript gets read as "some minstrel's working copy" — good for listeners interested in manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction.

1:03 The most complete version is an English manuscript
The Song of Roland is a French epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre Chanson de Geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century French cultural hegemony to regions including Britain. But its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from France proper — it is an English manuscript, catalogued as Oxford Digby 23. This manuscript was at some point bound together with a completely unrelated book, which is why it is called Digby 23 B, and A is that "other book." Nobody knows who bound them together; possibly some monk felt both were his favourite books.

3:05 Every stanza is a camera position
The poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood changes, you change laisse. The whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut at performance into four plus six: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six syllables fall, overall close to iambic turning into trochaic. Chanted over and over it becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs to four thousand lines — hours of recitation.

7:27 At peak emotion, the same action is performed three times
This kind of epic has a convention that is hard for any reteller to handle: when the action is especially intense or the emotion especially strong, several consecutive laisses will tell the same action from three angles — a slow-motion sequence in poetic form. Roland's refusal to blow the oliphant, for instance, is told three times with almost no gap between them. This is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — "Roland dies, his soul ascends" is followed directly by "the emperor arrives at Roncevaux."

9:29 The end of the manuscript leaves the performer's name
Digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. Line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; Turoldus will not tell more." This line comes before Charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, I cannot go on. The name Turoldus does not appear in the poem and is not a known scribe, so scholars lean towards him being the owner of this manuscript, the performer of this performance.

10:31 Pocket-size dimensions give away that it was a working copy
The manuscript measures only about six and a half inches by four and a half — a pocket copy you could carry on your person, not a wealthy man's finely bound volume. It is itself heavily worn and not refined, and it contains some small annotations of unclear meaning. Together these features point to an itinerant professional performer: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator of a troupe, with someone in front of him doing the physical acting. Such people were jongleurs — the origin of the later word juggler.

12:31 The dialect pins this performer to England
The manuscript is not in the French of central France, nor continental French, but in Anglo-Norman, which suggests the performer was probably Anglo-Norman, performing in Britain or at least in Normandy. The dialect features are very specific: continental French O and OU are replaced by U, so Roland becomes Rulant, l'or becomes l'ur; Anglo-Norman French is also dropping final soft e. These changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven.

14:34 Accent drift alone can date a manuscript
Scholars' grasp of this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. The method is similar to scholars reconstructing Shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. Poetry is especially suited to this reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. For many jongleurs, French was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent — and they spelled by sound.

17:40 A French epic, an English artefact
Although this is a French poem about an old French king, the manuscript is an English thing, performed for Britons at the time. There is no equally complete other manuscript to compare line by line, but there are abundant records of The Song of Roland being sung before and after this copy, and scholars can use them to judge where this performer departed from what the genre should look like. The episode goes on to cover the poem's symbolic system, how its audience was constructed, and what the music sounded like.

item.title: The Army Secretary Resigns: The People Who Know How to Fight Get Cleared Out First
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-chinatalk-陆军部长辞职-最会打仗的人先被清掉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-chinatalk-陆军部长辞职-最会打仗的人先被清掉/
item.description: Twenty-five years after 9/11, the US military has been on a treadmill: budgets eaten by war, transformation forced through on cheap technology, and the officers who actually understand tech and are willing to take risk are being cleared out batch by batch.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the US military has been on a treadmill: budgets eaten by war, transformation forced through on cheap technology, and the officers who actually understand tech and are willing to take risk are being cleared out batch by batch.

The first half — the 9/11 reckoning and Army personnel insider material — is dense; the second half, on AI battlefields and model distillation, is more casual chat, so you can listen to just the first half.

3:03 The war on terror ate the money for military transformation
Before 9/11 the US military was transforming as Rumsfeld demanded, and the expectation was a relatively comfortable budget environment in which new technology could be pushed into the force gradually. Then GWAT arrived, all available resources were sucked into the war, and the transformation directive remained while the money was gone. Hence a run of procurement disasters: the Army's Future Combat Systems, the Navy's Ford-class carrier, Littoral Combat Ship, DDG-1000 Zumwalt, and the CGX that was simply never built. Brian's judgment is that the technology jumped too far, the investment was nowhere near enough, and everyone was distracted supporting a war that had just started, so these programs were doomed. The troubles with today's B-21 and F-35 trace back to this period too.

5:22 Twenty-five years on a treadmill, never actually stopping
Tony points out that op-tempo never stopped after it started in 2001: 12-month, 15-month deployment rotations, and the National Guard is still deploying at home and abroad today. Killing Bin Laden in 2011 could have been a high point, but nothing changed afterward — deployments continued, and through the fall of Kabul, they were still deploying. Nobody has fully calculated what 25 straight years in that state costs an army. Brian adds a mechanism: conventional forces used to train at home, reset, and move through a training progression, and that rhythm disappeared, replaced by "preparing for the next deployment," so there is no time to test new technology or study new ways of fighting.

7:31 MRAP thinking: use a bigger truck to stop an anti-tank missile
Brian gives an example absurd in its specificity. In Syria the threat was not IEDs but ATGMs (anti-tank guided weapons, similar to Russian TOW variants). The commander's reflex was still to stuff everyone into MRAPs — making the vehicle bigger, which made it easier for the ATGM to find the target, while MRAP armor cannot stop munitions designed to penetrate tanks. His conclusion: risk calculus from the war-on-terror era has sunk so deep that commanders cannot reconceptualize even a small tactical adjustment. This is also the direct consequence of why so many commanders today struggle to adapt to Ukraine and the Lisko battlefield, and cannot imagine how tactics will change.

9:37 Get used to zero casualties and you can't accept that people will die
Brian says that after 9/11 the US military became increasingly risk- and casualty-averse. The Littoral Combat Ship debate is the specimen: opponents said the ship couldn't take a hit and would be sunk the moment a war started; the original proposers answered that it was never going to be sent into a major war, and if it got sunk in a surprise attack, that was the risk you take for serving. That logic was completely unacceptable on Capitol Hill — Iraq and Afghanistan pushed casualties far below the levels of past wars, everyone got used to it, and so they cannot accept that against a peer adversary a lot of people will probably die. The result is continuing to build "Death Star"-style big ships and big platforms, hoping they can protect themselves, rather than going with smaller, more distributed routes that accept a different risk structure.

10:39 Twenty-five years encircling Iran without building a network
Brian says this is the most important lesson he took from 9/11, and it came from a friend's reminder: for 25 years the US has basically surrounded Iran, and the CIA's and part of special operations' job is to develop networks and identify people who could oppose an oppressive regime, in case a moment of change comes. But when the shooting against Iran started six months ago, it looked like very little network and capability building had been done in those 25 years. The reason is a mental shift: GWAT focused on counterinsurgency and catching bad guys, not the long-term unconventional warfare of pre-positioning the environment for a future conflict — how to support an insurgency inside a regime you might one day want to overthrow. In his words, everyone was too busy stabilizing the situation rather than destabilizing.

13:53 Driscoll resigns, and from here on it's all acting officials
Tony recaps: George was relieved, Driscoll went to the White House, said "everything is terrible," and resigned that same week. The backdrop is the Army being meddled with back and forth by OSD and the Secretary of the Army's office, plus personality clashes. What he hears is that Congress will not confirm anyone else Pete nominates, so either they swap in someone both the White House and Congress can accept but Pete dislikes, or they just keep using acting officials. He judges this is the start of the rest of this administration being "stuck in acting positions": after the midterms the House flips at least, the Senate either flips or goes 50:50, nobody has the energy to push this kind of person through, and so acting officials, continued OSD meddling, and low morale will persist.

14:54 The drone battalion is disbanded, and the ability to experiment goes with it
The Army decided around the same time to dissolve its newly created drone battalion — a battalion that was supposed to absorb Ukraine's experience directly and then work out how to embed it in infantry battalions. Tony concedes there is a good argument that "it shouldn't exist in only one battalion": concentrating lessons in one central warehouse strips every commander of the responsibility to think about their own organization. But his worry is that the Army still needs a unit that can run experiments, run tests, and allow failure; cutting it in the name of "uniformity" loses the ability to experiment, and the force will stand still. He also names Chris Donahue as sacrificed: a commander widely recognized as understanding technology, its effects, and how to run international partnerships, done away with because of the Abbey Gate bombing (not his fault) and a photo a reporter took.

21:03 Confidence is lost in layers, by rank
Tony breaks morale down by rank: junior officers are still early, but already thinking "garrison isn't what I signed up for," and if you're not garrisoned you're going out to get shot at with missiles; the field-grade level is starting to agonize over whether they have to make political decisions just to stay in; the senior field-grade and junior general officer level is basically "all in or burned out." He says the whole force is tired, and this doesn't look like the Army they joined. And in interviewees' telling, the Iran war is more of a tipping point than Donahue's departure — many O-4s and O-5s he knows supported this administration and are furious after the Donahue affair. Brian adds: people like Donahue are the true product of elite selection, and cutting them makes you doubt the claim that promotion is "by ability alone."

item.title: AI researchers sped up 10x in two years, but RSI may be easier than being a paralegal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-dwarkesh-ai-研究员两年提速-10-倍-但-rsi-可能比当律师助理更容易/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-dwarkesh-ai-研究员两年提速-10-倍-但-rsi-可能比当律师助理更容易/
item.description: RSI is an accumulating task: in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch. A law-firm paralegal, by contrast, has to remember shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things — a non-stationary distribution.
item.content:encoded:
RSI is an accumulating task: in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch. A law-firm paralegal, by contrast, has to remember shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things — a non-stationary distribution.

The three researchers' disagreements about RSI, continual learning and RL generalisation are very concrete, and the second half's mechanistic explanation of mid-training and signal-to-noise is the most valuable part of the episode.

0:00 A model looks smart, then a month later looks dumb again
John Schulman describes a recurring loop: a new model comes out, people are blown away and say "this is AGI," but after about a month of use it starts to look dumb again. This loop may keep repeating, and it's hard to predict how many more times. His mechanism: capability won't explode right now, because when doing research and engineering you still get stuck on bottlenecks — even if a model can write far more code than a person, it won't give you a 100x productivity gain. Dwarkesh opens by asking: if by 2036 there's no crazy alien superintelligence, what's the most likely technical reason? Beren Millidge's default answer is a Moravec-paradox-style continuation — AI does superbly at whatever humans put into a benchmark or environment, but a stubborn sim-to-real gap always stands in the way.

18:39 Distillation is the only force against centralisation
John Schulman sees distillation as the main force countering the centralisation trend: anything learnable through RL can be distilled easily, because the number of bits is small and a little data suffices. But he stresses distillation is not trivial — when distilling with supervised learning the prompt distribution matters enormously, and you need a real, broad prompt distribution. He mentions something that has recently surfaced: some Chinese companies may be running router services that let Chinese users access otherwise-blocked US frontier models, and these services collect and sell data, which is an extremely useful dataset for distillation because it gives a perfect prompt distribution. Charlie O'Neill draws a concrete prediction from this: frontier labs may not have much of an edge left in RL environments.

44:38 RSI is an accumulating task; being a lawyer is not
Charlie O'Neill splits tasks into two kinds: accumulating and non-stationary. RSI is accumulating — in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch, and once attention, mixture of experts or GRPO is discovered you just add it to the training stack without going back to the start. The real world is not accumulating: a law-firm paralegal has to remember the shifting relationships among all the important people in the firm and all the tacit ways of doing things — a non-stationary distribution. Dwarkesh's summary is that "RSI happens to be easier than being a paralegal, which is too bad." If labs conclude RSI is an accumulating task, more compute will tilt that way.

52:00 Continual learning is stuck on catastrophic forgetting
Charlie O'Neill says the outer loop of pouring data into mid-training at large scale and large batch does work, but at the micro level — a model doing several hundred consecutive micro-updates for one law firm — every method collapses: SFT on successful trajectories causes catastrophic forgetting and general capability degrades; on-policy distillation pushes that boundary a bit further out but eventually yields too. RL is good at instilling capabilities, bad at instilling knowledge. Beren Millidge thinks this is mainly a technical problem, not a capacity problem: a model of the same size pretrained from scratch on all the data is simply better, and the bottleneck is plasticity and catastrophic forgetting, with no good way to stop old data being forgotten.

59:46 Data explains 12x, architecture only 3.7x
Dwarkesh and Princeton's Jerry Han ran a grid experiment: pairing training recipes and datasets from 2019 to now in every combination, GPT-2 with the latest Ultra-FineWeb, Delphi with an old dataset like Pile, running the whole grid. The conclusion is that data gives roughly a 12.0x compute-efficiency gain, while architecture improvements give only about 3.7x, and at very small scale. Charlie O'Neill says the big internet chunk has already been eaten, useful things won't keep growing at the same rate, and there's probably only a pile of 0.1% loss reductions left. He notes someone at Epoch estimated 3x per year since 2019, over 2000x cumulative, and the missing 100x probably comes from post-training.

1:03:00 RL needs a curriculum; pretraining does not
Beren Millidge says this comes back to the RL signal problem: RL is currently bad at exploration, and if the model can't get it in 128 rollouts there's basically no learning signal, so RL needs curricula while pretraining needs none at all. Charlie O'Neill adds: the pretraining signal is already in Common Crawl, the problem is just filtering out noise, which can be automated; but once you get to mid-training and post-training the signal simply isn't in the raw data, and no amount of filtering will extract it — there isn't a Millennium Prize proof hiding in Common Crawl waiting to be filtered out. You have to get the bits from elsewhere: have people write out reasoning traces, construct environments, or use human data from deployment.

1:18:03 Most of RL's success comes from mid-training
Beren Millidge says what's underrated is mid-training: pretraining on synthetic reasoning data and environments, warm-starting the model to where it has almost completed 80% of the path to the final RL checkpoint, with RL only fine-tuning the policy on top. So it doesn't need to learn these behaviours from scratch, and a few bits per episode suffice. He also stresses that these bits have a far higher signal-to-noise ratio than ordinary pretraining — in SFT you have to match another model's reasoning process token by token, which pours in too many bits about "how it thinks" and drowns the signal; RL's objective ignores all the other bits and keeps only "did it get the answer right."

1:28:32 One year or three, the difference is long-tail chores
Asked when you could hire a drop-in remote white-collar worker, Charlie O'Neill says if it has to operate a browser, probably a few years; if it can be given Slack and programmatic access, probably a year. Beren Millidge says full generality might take three years, but organisations will actively reshape themselves to be more AI-friendly, so 80-90% is reachable before then. The substance of the disagreement is the long tail: some chores humans can do will take the model a long time. Charlie gives the example that the model won't "yell at people" to push work forward — it's too nice. John Schulman points out that human remote workers already vary enormously in quality, and on Upwork it's often hard to get someone doing a software project to take feedback seriously; in some cases the pre-AI version is worse than today's AI.

item.title: The Clippers Used Fake Endorsements to Skirt the Salary Cap, and the NBA's Law Firm Found More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-moneystuff-快船用假代言绕工资帽-nba-请律所查出了更多/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-moneystuff-快船用假代言绕工资帽-nba-请律所查出了更多/
item.description: Wachtell's independent investigation did not clear the Clippers — it made the scandal bigger: beyond Aspiration, there is a string of fake endorsements funded by the Clippers that ultimately flowed to Kawhi Leonard.
item.content:encoded:
Wachtell's independent investigation did not clear the Clippers — it made the scandal bigger: beyond Aspiration, there is a string of fake endorsements funded by the Clippers that ultimately flowed to Kawhi Leonard.

The first half is dense with sports-scandal detail; the second half — Apollo's "jerk premium" and the Cede & Co stock custody mechanism — is the part that is actually worth money.

2:04 The Clippers used fake endorsements to get around the salary cap
The Clippers first paid millions of dollars to a company called Aspiration Partners, nominally for vague environmental services; Aspiration then paid that money to Kawhi Leonard in the form of endorsement fees, while Leonard did almost no endorsing. When Pablo Torre first reported it, the claim was still disputed, and the Clippers kept denying it, but the investigation the NBA commissioned from Wachtell Lipton basically confirmed it — and found more similar arrangements.

4:09 Even the scoreboard company was pulled in to move the money
What the Wachtell report found was not just the Aspiration payment. The Clippers also paid "consulting fees" to companies that provided no consulting services at all, including the company that made the scoreboard for their arena. The method: the Clippers would pay a consulting fee, then call and ask for a higher purchase price on the scoreboard, with the clear expectation that the other side would pass the money on to Kawhi Leonard. The money went in a circle, and the ultimate purpose was still to give the star a raise.

7:09 An independent law firm investigation is not there to clear you
Max had assumed an outside law firm's independent investigation was meant to produce a "clean bill of health" after a scandal, but the Wachtell report made things look worse. Matt offers a more cynical explanation: the classic use of a law firm investigation, under the shadow of a DOJ or regulatory probe, is to hand over some "bad apple" as a scapegoat so the company gets credit for cooperating. But this time there was no DOJ pressure to shut down the NBA, the NBA seems to have given Wachtell a lot of room, and Wachtell clearly had a lot of fun investigating.

10:14 Once the DAT premium vanished, the arbitrage ran in reverse
Empery Digital was originally an electric motorcycle company, and in July 2025 it transformed into a digital asset treasury company (DAT), stockpiling about $500 million of bitcoin, with its stock at one point trading at a premium to its holdings. The logic: put $1 of bitcoin into a DAT and it becomes $2 of stock. But the premium quickly disappeared and DATs began trading at a discount, so the arbitrage flipped — use $0.90 of stock to buy $1 of bitcoin, buy the DAT, break it up, sell the bitcoin. DAT activism was born.

17:20 Is a shareholder shorting bitcoin disloyal
One of the core disputes in the Empery case: an activist buys discounted DAT stock while shorting an equal amount of bitcoin, making itself delta neutral and earning only the discount convergence. The company argues this must be disclosed, because the other shareholders are all theoretically long bitcoin, while these people are bitcoin neutral, their interests are not aligned, and they should not be eligible to run for the board. Matt thinks the argument is "wrong, but only accidentally wrong": if a DAT is a vehicle for believers to hold bitcoin (like Strategy), it makes sense; but most DAT shareholders are the same hedge funds, all of whom came for the premium and are unhappy about the discount, so their interests are actually aligned.

23:26 Cede & Co holds most American stocks
Matt mentions a fact in his column that most people do not know: most shares of most American companies are registered in the name of Cede & Co, which is DTC's nominee. A 1998 report said Cede & Co held 83% of all US stocks; DTC now custodies about $74 trillion of stocks. When you hold shares through Robinhood, what actually happens is that Robinhood has a record on DTC's ledger, and Cede & Co is on the company's shareholder register. The system grew out of the efficiency revolution of the 1960s and 1970s, when paper stock certificates were centralised in one place and only name changes were recorded.

27:31 Robinhood's tokenisation is not an on-chain shareholder register
Tokenised stocks can mean many things, and one ideal version is this: every company maintains a public blockchain shareholder register, no longer needing intermediaries like DTC or Robinhood, and the company can build a direct relationship with its shareholders. But that is not what Robinhood did — it bought AMC stock itself, then issued derivative securities on-chain representing those shares and sold them to overseas investors, effectively "making its own copy of AMC stock". AMC's Adam Aaron was unhappy, and Vlad Tenev shot back, "What's the concern?"

31:35 Apollo pays 100 basis points for its "aggressive" reputation
A paper measures private equity sponsors' reputations in three ways: having ChatGPT and Claude rank the most aggressive PE firms; looking at who has done liability management exercises (quasi-coercive debt swaps); and putting Apollo in one bucket by itself and the other 24 firms in another. The conclusion: the most aggressive sponsors' portfolio companies borrow at noticeably higher yields, Apollo's loans are about 100 basis points more expensive than other sponsors', and the sample's average yield is 717 basis points. Matt calls it the "jerk premium" or the "aggression premium" — creditors expect to be squeezed, so they charge upfront.

item.title: The foldable isn't the future of the phone — it's a two-in-one for a subset of people
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cn1b5ef7-折叠屏不是手机的未来-是给一部分人的二合一/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cn1b5ef7-折叠屏不是手机的未来-是给一部分人的二合一/
item.description: Foldables have sold into the tens of millions, but the inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time. They won't replace the slab phone; for people who want a phone-plus-iPad two-in-one they're a plus, and for everyone else they're a minus that costs you grip and performance.
item.content:encoded:
Foldables have sold into the tens of millions, but the inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time. They won't replace the slab phone; for people who want a phone-plus-iPad two-in-one they're a plus, and for everyone else they're a minus that costs you grip and performance.

A solo episode with a product manager's eye that covers the real experience of using a foldable, the business logic behind Apple entering, and the judgment that phone form factors will diverge rather than converge. Medium information density; the back half is worth more than the front half.

12:17 The foldable's home turf is China and nowhere else
In 2025, China's full-year foldable shipments broke ten million units, with Huawei taking 70% — a crushing share. But globally, China is the largest single market, accounting for more than 40% of shipments. In other words, this category isn't evenly distributed the way other phone form factors are; its core user is the Chinese boss holding a Huawei foldable in first class and at social occasions. On the broad market, foldables are only 2.5% of global phone shipments, and only 15% of Huawei's own phone shipments.

20:23 The inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time
Liu Fei used foldables as his daily driver for over half a month, and in the end he didn't want to keep them. The biggest problem wasn't the crease, the camera, or the battery — it was the scenario. The inner screen doesn't get opened much: it's unstable in one hand and prone to shaking, and it's more for two-handed use — but in that scenario he'd already be carrying a 10-inch iPad. A Vivo vice president said at a launch event that foldables keep getting better, but the core way they're used is no different from seven years ago, and many users use the inner screen less than 30% of the time. His analogy: it's like carrying a phone case with a built-in power bank — your phone's weight goes up permanently, but most of the time you don't need to charge, so you'd be better off carrying a separate external power bank.

23:25 Once it gets wider, scrolling feeds actually gets worse
To accommodate the outer screen, wide-expanding foldables like the Huawei Pure X Max and the Apple iPhone Door got wider, and scrolling feeds on them becomes very bad. Xiaohongshu is fine, because it's been adapted; but when scrolling Meituan to filter restaurants or Taobao to filter shops, the information that fits on each screen suddenly shrinks. This isn't purely an adaptation problem, it's an aspect-ratio problem: list feeds run vertically, so widening is meaningless — the height shrinks, and you see less at once. He recalls that ordering takeout on Meituan, he could only see three restaurants at a time.

29:33 76% more area, yet widescreen video looks smaller
A large foldable is almost square when unfolded, which is a disaster for watching video and photos. By screen area, opening the inner screen adds 76%, nearly double; but if you're watching a widescreen film, the foldable's inner screen actually loses about 10% of its effective area, because it can't fit it. Watching 16:9 content does get bigger, but only by 20%, which is fairly limited. Wide-expanding foldables have more sensible dimensions and higher effective area, but a 16:10 wide-expanding foldable playing 16:9 video still has 10% black bars top and bottom. The point isn't that area naturally increases — it's what you actually want to do with the inner screen.

37:38 Who the two-in-one is a plus for
Liu Fei says the most important decision logic for whether to buy a foldable is: does it add to or subtract from your existing experience. He has a full set of devices himself — a Windows PC for gaming, a MacBook for work, an iPad for shows — so a foldable is pointless for him. But for many young people, the phone is their only computing device, and a lot of work happens on the phone and offline, so a bigger screen makes the experience much better. Salespeople who travel often and need to present a PPT to a client in a café also get a much better result from the inner screen than the outer one. Put another way: what you're buying isn't a slab phone that turns into a tablet, it's a foldable iPad mini.

45:47 Without AirPods there'd be no Chinese podcast market
Liu Fei says the Apple Watch and AirPods developed during Cook's tenure are both world-changing products, and AirPods especially so: without AirPods ushering in the era of Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones, you could say there'd be no podcast market — especially no Chinese podcast market. Chinese podcasts took off in sync with Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones — because with noise cancelling, you can hear clearly what someone is saying while commuting, working out, or doing chores. Before that, those scenarios were usually for listening to music, or to content with very low information density.

57:04 Apple's killer move is migrating the iPad ecosystem
On hardware, the iPhone Door doesn't have such an overwhelming advantage; it uses materials from mature supply chains, weighs 254 grams, and isn't perceptibly that different from Android flagship foldables. The core advantage is that Apple has the iPad: since the iPad launched in 2010, its 4:3 ratio has accumulated a huge content ecosystem, and many apps were already optimised well enough for that ratio before foldable phones even existed, so they can be ported directly to the iPhone Door. For Android, that's a crushing level of ecosystem migration. Apple has also done a lot of optimisation on one-handed interaction, putting frequently used buttons on the dominant-hand side — that's a system-level design, and it's relatively easy for developers to follow and adapt to.

1:08:09 How you define success decides whether it succeeds
Whether the iPhone Door succeeds depends on how you define success. If you define it as replacing the slab phone, it's nearly impossible; if you define it as becoming a product line that keeps selling, it's very possible. A few million units in the first generation is no problem, and it might even reach ten million; JD reservations have already passed 500,000. Liu Fei says phone form factors won't converge, they'll diverge: the slab phone is the only form factor the whole world would vote for, but other form factors will keep existing and keep differentiating, at every price point and in every shape. Foldables won't replace slab phones, even if performance, experience and price were exactly the same, because a substantial number of people simply have no need to open the inner screen.

item.title: Americans Suddenly Love Japan, Not Because It's Cheap, But Because It's Normal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-searchengine-美国人突然爱上日本-不是因为便宜-是因为它太正常了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-searchengine-美国人突然爱上日本-不是因为便宜-是因为它太正常了/
item.description: The real driver of Japan's tourism boom isn't the exchange rate, it's the functionality of public space—clean subways, on time, no trash. What American visitors experience in Tokyo is a society where entropy has been paused.
item.content:encoded:
The real driver of Japan's tourism boom isn't the exchange rate, it's the functionality of public space—clean subways, on time, no trash. What American visitors experience in Tokyo is a society where entropy has been paused.

This episode uses expert interviews and a listener survey to break down 'why everyone's going to Japan' into six verifiable reasons. The second half, contrasting Japanese craft culture with American dysfunction, is especially worth hearing.

1:05 An Excel sheet of 119 visitors
The questioner, Lisa, is a Japanese person living in Tokyo. She made a visitor calendar from November 2022 to April 2026, with green cells marking when someone visited. She counted 119 people, 96 of them her own guests, averaging one person every five days, or 20% of all her days. She says she spends all her free time helping visiting friends plan their trips. This data visualization is itself evidence of a problem out of control, and the starting point for the question this episode answers.

8:34 Japan is poor in resources, rich in story
Roland Kelts argues the first reason for American interest in Japan isn't economic, it's story. He says Japan has almost no natural resources, no oil, very little land, only small rice paddies, but an astonishing culture of story. The world's first novel is Japan's The Tale of Genji, a thousand years old. Through manga, anime, and the internet, the world discovered this narrative ability. This didn't start in the 90s; Roland says there were two earlier waves: Japonisme in late 19th-century Europe, and the Beat and hippie fascination with Zen and Buddhist concepts in the 50s and 60s.

15:05 America used to fear Japan
David Marks points out that for seventy years after WWII, mainstream America viewed Japan with fear, not affection. Before 1945 Japan was an enemy nation, then seen as a developing country rebuilding. In the 70s and 80s it became anxiety about Japan's economic power, with Michael Crichton's Rising Sun casting Japan as the villain. After the Cold War, there was even a CIA position paper discussing whether Japan should be the next enemy. When Japan's bubble burst in the 90s, America felt a sense of relief. When David moved to Japan in 2003, having a friend visit was a big event of the year, because almost no one came.

24:29 The government deliberately made Japan cheap
The third wave was a government plan. In 2003, Junichiro Koizumi launched the Visit Japan campaign, aiming to raise tourists from 5 million to 10 million a year, with ads full of Western stereotypes of geisha, cherry blossoms, and temples. But what really worked was Shinzo Abe deliberately weakening the yen in the 2010s, intended to help exports, which made hotels and restaurants cheap for foreigners.
