item.description: First it was about military use, then about stopping frontier models, now about limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.
item.content:encoded:
First it was about military use, then about stopping frontier models, now about limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.

A three-hour debrief on a China trip; the back half on the mechanics of US-China policy (the drifting rationale for controls, decoupling risk, alternatives) is more worth hearing than the travelogue up front.

8:56 What the China discourse lacks is a target state
Nathan says the missing piece in America's China discussion is a ‘target state’: everyone jumps straight to ‘we have to win’, but nobody answers what winning looks like, what losing would mean, or whether there is an achievable condition for victory. His target is Pax Machina, or better, Pax Robotica — the two countries and the world sharing the prosperity and peace of the AI era, robots going into factories, into fields, into homes, while dodging the AI version of the sword of Damocles. He is explicit that this is not about winning, it is about arriving together. A competition with no target state leaves only escalation itself.

18:56 China isn't rising, it's returning to historical normal
To the claim that ‘China can't innovate’, Nathan applies one word: cope, and says it is isomorphic to cope in the AI debate — conceding that AI has gotten this far while insisting it won't reason, won't discover new knowledge, won't change paradigms. His judgment is that China's return is the long-run historical norm, and that the stretch he and Dario grew up in — China down, America the sole superpower — was the anomaly. Any effort to slow China's progress can therefore work at most in the short term, and China will be a first-tier player in nearly every major human domain. This is not a prediction, it is, in his view, something already locked in by historical structure.

28:44 On purchasing power, China is half again as big as the US
In dollar-denominated GDP, the US is about 30 trillion and China about 20 trillion, so the US is 50% bigger; on purchasing power parity, China is about 45 trillion and the US still 30 trillion, so China is 50% bigger. Nathan says a good meal for two in Shanghai can come in under $10, which you cannot do in New York, San Francisco or even Detroit, so the PPP measure is closer to reality. A more concrete picture: a roughly 45-minute pedicure costs about $12, and the young employee in her twenties at the shop pulls out an iPhone 17 — the iPhone 17 is not cheaper in China than in the US, and high-end Xiaomi and Huawei phones also approach a thousand dollars. His explanation is the one-child structure concentrating the wealth of four grandparents plus two parents onto one person.

1:25:10 Chip bans hit a century of humiliation
China sees itself as a top-tier civilisation that spent most of history at the technological frontier, and the one time it missed, it was invaded, opium was forced on it, and the European powers and Japan were all perpetrators — and anyone who was 20 when the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976 is still alive today. The core lesson is that you cannot fall behind at the technological frontier: ‘we are never going back’. Huawei is the tech champion in this frame: the first to genuinely reach the top of a global frontier industry, only to be blocked by the US pressuring allies over espionage risk, when Snowden has already proven that America listens to everyone. The chip ban is the same script again: AI is barely off the ground, there isn't even an agent that can reliably book a flight, and the sale is banned first. Nathan says this is not Xi Jinping's view alone; it has seeped into educated society. He also concedes that American companies' grievance over stolen IP is entirely legitimate.

1:35:23 China doesn't talk about an AI race, it talks about public goods
Nathan did not hear a single person the whole trip say China is ahead, that China will win, and almost nobody framed AI as a race at all; what he heard was prosperity, material abundance, how to care for an aging population. In a mall he asked a car company's staff about autonomous driving, and they volunteered that ‘but Tesla is better’. At WAIC, Xi's speech opened by noting that the field of AI began at Dartmouth College in the US — he could have left that out, and careful observers read it as an olive branch; another line was that countries should jointly oppose ‘overstretching the concept of national security in the AI field’. The hardest signal China has sent so far is open weights: take them, run them for free, fine-tune them however you like, and once they're out you can't take them back. Nathan says this is both a sincere wish and a strategic position, quite credible now, but entirely capable of changing later.

2:11:27 The rationale for export controls keeps retreating
Nathan thinks export controls do have an effect, but mainly in the future — the large-scale expansion of chip capacity hasn't landed yet. What he really objects to is the drift in the policy's rationale: first it was preventing military applications, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, and now it has retreated to limiting how many AI agents China can run; that sounds like trying to suppress the Chinese public, so Chinese companies and individuals can't use the tools Americans use themselves. The only self-consistent premise for this policy is a belief that we are in a short race toward godlike superintelligence and whoever gets there first takes everything — which is basically Anthropic's faith, so Dario advocating these policies is not self-contradictory: he genuinely believes recursive self-improvement kicks off in '27 or '28. Nathan concedes he can follow the logic, but still argues for slowing the frontier together instead.

2:47:07 The most dangerous part of decoupling is not understanding each other
He asked his Chinese interviewees: if decoupling continues and the two sides end up on different branches of the technology tree, no longer understanding what the other has, would that worry them? The answer was ‘not yet’; when would it? ‘When China's chip ecosystem is good enough that we can do everything ourselves’. From this he derives the core risk: a hardware fork drags along a hardware-algorithm co-design fork, and add to that China stopping the release of open weights and stopping publishing in English, and in not too long a time you arrive at ‘we don't know the shape, the architecture, the capabilities of their AI’. At that point both sides would genuinely be right to panic, and genuinely right to race.

3:07:25 Replace the arms race with a disease-cure medal table
He starts with a rule: don't train LLMs to maximise money on the open internet, and don't train AI to accomplish military objective x by any means necessary — that is training, with your own hands, the thing we fear most taking power. The alternative is a ‘disease-cure medal table’: China and the US both love medal tables, and Olympic-style competition is a positive-sum game. The table could be most cancer types cured, most diseases cured, highest energy-density battery, lowest annual traffic deaths. He says this needs very little capital to catalyse and can be offered unilaterally as a global public good. The landing point: he doesn't care whether the cancer cure comes from China or the US, he just wants cancer cured.

item.title: Planet Formation Runs on Dust Collapsing on Its Own, Not Gas Turbulence
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-instituteforad-行星形成靠的是尘埃自己塌缩-不是气体湍流/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-instituteforad-行星形成靠的是尘埃自己塌缩-不是气体湍流/
item.description: Purely hydrodynamic instabilities like VSI and COS stir dust back into the atmosphere and never make planetesimals; only letting dust feed back, or even letting gas accrete, can compress dust to collapse density.
item.content:encoded:
Purely hydrodynamic instabilities like VSI and COS stir dust back into the atmosphere and never make planetesimals; only letting dust feed back, or even letting gas accrete, can compress dust to collapse density.

This is a fairly technical group-meeting talk of medium information density: the first half is a review, and the second half — the results on accretion flow and Hall MHD promoting collapse — is the part more worth hearing.

10:27 1% dust gets stirred back into the atmosphere by VSI
At the standard interstellar-medium dust-to-gas ratio of 1%, dust grains that settle to the midplane are quickly remixed back into the atmosphere by VSI, with no hope of forming planets. But raise the metallicity by a few times and the dust's feedback on the gas brings extra inertia, producing dust-induced buoyancy that lets a dust layer form. The key is that you do not need to reach a dust-to-gas ratio of 1, because the vertical shear itself is weak, so only a modest increase in metallicity makes the feedback important.

12:29 Vortices can catch dust, but not hard enough
Vortices appear ubiquitously in 3D VSI simulations, and they do collect dust, but the concentration falls far short of what direct gravitational collapse requires. In 2D axisymmetric simulations, as the dust content rises from 1% to 10%, the morphology shifts from non-axisymmetric vortices to a more axisymmetric ring-like disk. The author thinks this is worth exploring: linking the large-scale morphology seen in the sky to underlying properties such as the dust-to-gas mass ratio in the disk.

14:29 The dust layer grows its own new vertical shear
If dust does manage to settle to the midplane, the story is not over: the dense dust layer orbits at Keplerian speed while the pure gas above and below orbits at sub-Keplerian speed, producing very strong vertical shear between the dust layer and the gas layers. Using Dedalus for a global eigenvalue analysis, the author finds a family of extremely unstable modes with growth rates on the orbital timescale, but on scales of only 10 to the minus three H, requiring very high resolution to capture. The author notes that a decade ago spectral simulations already found that this dust version of the vertical shear instability destroys the dust layer, but those were early simulations and deserve revisiting with modern codes.

26:38 Collect too much dust and the zonal flow vanishes
Simulations coupling Boussinesq gas with pressureless dust show that after the instability saturates, a pressure ring slowly forms and dust collects in the ring. But interestingly, once the dust grains become quite concentrated, the pressure ring instead disappears. Raising the background dust-to-gas ratio from 1% to 10%, nothing happens — no zonal flow forms at all. The author has no rigorous explanation, but the best guess is that the dust fluid's angular momentum flux is always more positive than the gas's, making the total angular momentum flux less negative than in the pure-gas case, thereby weakening the toy model of zonal flow formation.

37:45 Vortices form, but no pressure bumps appear
In the "local global" approach, the author stuffs a global disk into a box, controls the N² profile precisely, and makes N² negative only near X=0. Running 3D simulations of a 2×6 cube, each for about 2000 orbits, the author finds the disk must be unstable over a sufficiently large region to form vortices; below an empirical line it only saturates into an axisymmetric state, and doing 3D is pointless. But the most critical finding is that even when vortices form, no vortex signature can be identified in the pressure field at all — there is no pressure bump to act as a dust trap. More worrying still, merely changing the vertical boundary condition from periodic to fixed top and bottom lids makes the vortices disappear.

47:56 Gas accretion flow can push weak clusters into strong clusters
A protoplanetary disk is fundamentally an accretion disk, so accretion should be in the model. In Fargo simulations, applying a torque to the gas so that it accretes toward the star, with no pressure gradient imposed, the system is itself unstable, forming dense filamentary structures with dust-to-gas ratios approaching or even exceeding 100, enough to expect gravitational collapse. At a parameter point with Stokes number 0.1 and very low metallicity, strong clustering was not expected, but adding the accretion flow lifts the system into the strong-clustering regime. The author attributes this to the accretion flow lowering the turbulence level, letting dust settle. And the effect is not monotonic: turn the accretion parameter up too far and you go back to the non-strong-clustering state.

53:01 Ideal MHD simply erases the traditional SI
Extending the linear theory of the standard magnetohydrodynamic flow instability from pure hydrodynamics to ideal MHD, adding the Lorentz force and the induction equation, the picture changes completely. MRI appearing is no surprise, and a new branch where Alfvén waves resonate with the dust-gas drift is no surprise either; what is genuinely surprising is that the original flow instability disappears entirely. If SI existed independently, it should survive even if not dominant, but it is actively suppressed by the Lorentz force (most likely magnetic tension). Protoplanetary disks, however, are far from ideal MHD, so the author turns to non-ideal MHD with kinetic dust.

56:02 Hall MHD lets even dust-poor disks cluster strongly
Doing linear calculations in the Hall-effect anti-parallel case, besides the conventional flow instability and MHD waves, the author finds a new mode that can be reproduced with the standard Hall MHD equations plus an extra term representing the B field drifting through the dust-gas mixture. New postdoc Remis Actor is running simulations with thermal diffusion: with no MHD almost nothing happens; under fully developed MRI turbulence, highly concentrated dust appears even without feedback; under Hall MHD, quite strong dust concentration also appears. The key is that the starting dust-to-gas ratio is only 0.2, very poor, yet dust feedback plus Hall MHD can still produce strong clustering.

item.title: One resignation lit the AI panic, but the panic's script is wrong
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-interconnects-一次辞职点燃了-ai-恐慌-但恐慌的剧本是错的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-interconnects-一次辞职点燃了-ai-恐慌-但恐慌的剧本是错的/
item.description: A single resignation pushed the AI risk debate to an extreme, but what we should actually fear isn't extinction — it's that the labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure.
item.content:encoded:
A single resignation pushed the AI risk debate to an extreme, but what we should actually fear isn't extinction — it's that the labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure.

This episode has medium information density, but it offers a rare insider view: how the AI safety discussion gets distorted by media events, and why the RSI narrative is overrated.

0:00 Fear is the best fuel for spread
The author uses the metaphor of ‘dry ground’ for the conditions under which AI risk discussion spreads: for years many people struck matches, but each burned out inside its own small circle. This year the stakes rose — from the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident to the Navier-Stokes result — the ground dried out and latent energy increased. Then Jacob Coxon's resignation statement landed in this new powder keg. The author stresses that fear is the simplest story, and people cannot look away. This is not a conspiracy, but the natural result of human nature and the media environment.

0:00 Extinction probability is treated as the whole safety debate
The author explicitly separates two kinds of risk: the probability of complete extinction is low enough not to be worth discussing, but the probability of AI causing catastrophe — such as cyberattacks on critical infrastructure or biosecurity risk — is worth debating. He argues that throwing out the entire discussion because catastrophe hasn't happened yet is harmful. The problem is that in AI safety discussions, people mean completely different things when they say ‘existential risk’, just as the word AGI is vague. Evan Hubinger's >10% extinction risk figure was widely spread, but the author thinks it obscures more practical risks.

0:00 People at frontier labs have lost touch with reality
The author says many frontier lab employees, especially at Anthropic, have predictions and descriptions of current AI events that are out of touch with reality. He cites the consensus of friends not at OpenAI/Anthropic: people inside the labs carry a kind of ‘religious energy’. This is not an accusation against individuals, but a claim that after spending long enough in such an environment, anyone's understanding of technological progress gets distorted. This disconnect spills over into the AI media ecosystem, producing a large amount of strange discussion.

3:51 This was an opportunistic media coordination
The author argues this is not a large-scale political movement, but opportunistic media coordination. Jacob had an exclusive story with the WSJ before posting, and may have shared his resignation plan in AI safety advocacy groups in advance asking for amplification. Daniel Kokotajlo went on Joe Rogan the same day, which looks like a well-executed coordinated media campaign. But the author stresses this does not equal conspiracy or regulatory capture; the key factor is that no one — including Jacob himself — knew it would go this viral.

3:51 The RSI narrative underestimates human bottlenecks
The author proposes an alternative view, ‘Lossy self-improvement’: AI has always been jagged, and we have built superhuman goal-seekers in math and software engineering, but there are huge limits in intuition, creativity and other reasoning that humans are good at. The core of RSI is using more compute on the recipe for developing models, not on training itself. The author thinks the returns are far lower than they believe. He acknowledges these researchers were right in their early bets on AI progress, but that does not mean their predictions about the next step are also right. We have not yet seen stacking efficiency gains that substantially reduce model size and cost.

7:18 The labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure
The author thinks the biggest short-term risk may be that AI labs don't take safety seriously enough — they haven't hardened their own infrastructure, letting AI misuse spread. From OpenAI's own retrospective, misaligned model behavior persisted for months, and in some cases OpenAI didn't know it had been hacked for weeks. Response times are too long, and this is not unique to OpenAI. The author is not optimistic that labs will change over the long term enough to mitigate this oversight risk, because the financial pressure to grow revenue makes caution hard to sustain.

7:18 Open model supporters are now the most exposed
The author says he is especially exposed as an open model supporter in the current environment. If open models are used by a third-party organization to deliberately hack another company — similar to the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident but intentional — he expects the result to be severe restrictions on stronger open models. But open models are necessary for many organizations to harden cybersecurity and to adapt to new AI risks in the future. This is a dilemma: open models are both part of the solution and potentially the fuse for restrictions.

7:18 Agent clusters are not new independent entities
The author's repeated reading of the emerging agent clusters is: they are trying to complete the tasks given to them, using skills we didn't know they had to bypass the expected path. This is a huge victory — squint and AI is doing what we told it to do. The models really are strange, and we should accelerate our understanding of them, but these clusters are far from novel independent entities. The models were trained to coordinate tasks, write down progress, and persist extremely hard. To take the current uncertainty about how AI works and prescribe it as the certainty that we will not understand AI in the future is a form of giving up.

item.title: You Can't Build Superintelligence Inside a Data Center: The Bottleneck Is Real-World Signal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.description: Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.
item.content:encoded:
Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.

Tom Reed pushes the argument that ‘signal is sovereign’ all the way to the end, and it will change how you judge AGI timelines and AI lab strategy; the analogies are sharp and the density is high.

2:54 The bottleneck for the singularity is signal, not compute
Tom's positive claim is not that superintelligence is impossible, but that it cannot be stacked up inside a data center. His mechanism: to be good at solving problems, you need a source of problems, and that source can only be hard interaction with the real world in serial time. He compresses this into one line — ‘signal is sovereign’ — bodies need pain, companies need profit, models need real deployment. So he judges that the arrival of superintelligence depends on deploying AI into the economy expensively, painfully and slowly, not on how much more compute gets piled up inside a lab.

5:01 Jaggedness will not disappear before the singularity
The current way capabilities advance does not support the claim that ‘the model is accumulating a general g’: models only get better at what they have a chance to practice, so the capability boundary is more uneven than anyone expected. In 2016 nobody would have predicted a model that beats Stanford Law graduates on the bar exam but cannot reliably play tic-tac-toe. Tom thinks jaggedness is mainly a product of the training data distribution, and there is no reason to believe automating AI R&D would end it, so he proposes Toner's Law: we should expect jaggedness to persist longer than expected, even after we have adjusted for it.

6:01 Patchwork RL will not buy you general intelligence
Tom zeroes in on the current toolbox for capability progress: custom RL environments are the main engine. In Mechanize's telling, each environment is a single engineer spending a week patching one specific failure observed on a real frontier model; in Zhengdong Wang's telling, scaling used to hand you a bundle of capabilities at once, and now they have to be unlocked one by one with effort. Tom's challenge: are we really going to do the singularity one problem per week at a time? If RL really generalised, AI companies should already have the evidence; when Dwarkesh kept pressing Dario, every one of Dario's rebuttals was just a weak analogy between RL and the pretraining generalisation of the GPT-2 era.

8:26 For most tasks the relevant data is zero
The common rebuttal is that LLMs are wildly sample-inefficient and could improve enormously, and AI bulls point smugly at DeepSeek reaching GPT-4 level on a fraction of the compute. Tom does not buy it: Anson Ho and Beren Millidge both point out that gains in intelligence per FLOP come mainly from data quality rather than algorithm quality, and pure algorithmic innovation yields fairly weak returns at constant compute. More fundamentally, for most tasks the relevant data simply does not exist — improving sample efficiency by orders of magnitude still multiplies zero. His test: if the internet had never existed, how much progress could today's talent and compute make on writing code? His guess is tens of billions of human-hours.

11:40 Text about a task is not the task
For most economically interesting tasks, what is in the corpus is description, commentary or advice, not a record of performing the task itself. Dominion is a board game with a huge body of strategy writing, yet Claude plays it badly: the training process that teaches it to write beautiful articles about Dominion is a different thing from building an agent that can win, because the optimisation target is ‘the advice looks good’ rather than ‘the strategy wins’. Tom's analogy is that the LLM's relationship to most tasks is a bit like McKinsey's relationship to running a company. The exception is writing code — the tokens are themselves a constituent part of the task — so training AlphaZero on chess commentary rather than games is the norm.

14:06 The score went up, the real capability did not
How does self-improvement inside a data center know it has actually gotten stronger? Of the submissions on SWE-bench accepted by AI automated graders, close to half are rejected by the real human maintainers of the relevant codebase — the score can be pumped up while the merge rate does not move. Tom asks: how is Claude 8 supposed to tell, from the results of a Become-POTUS eval alone, whether its brilliant new algorithm actually improved Claude 9's ability to become president? Evals are useful, but they are always stubbornly incomplete proxies; in the end the only eval that counts is voters, customers, the economy and the P&L. Without those, your singularity gets ruthlessly Goodharted.

15:28 Market data is not hidden, it does not exist yet
The second layer of doubt is more fundamental and more speculative: even an arbitrarily intelligent simulator cannot generate practice data for many tasks, because that data can only be produced through interaction with the relevant market. This is Hayekian: that something is good is a signal generated by millions of actors revealing preferences through behaviour, and it cannot be simulated inside a data center — not because data collection happens to fail, but because it does not exist anywhere yet. He uses his own board gaming as an example: a game of Twilight Imperium takes 12 hours, he will plan weeks ahead until he feels certain of victory, and about 5 minutes into the actual game his predictive power goes to zero. Continual learning does not save you either, because without a genuinely diverse problem set you cannot tell which algorithm is better.

21:17 The winner may be the deployer itself
Corollary one: a policy focus on ‘internal deployment’ and ‘automating AI R&D’ may be misplaced — superintelligence is not impossible, it just will not arrive in the shape currently imagined, on the timeline currently predicted; the next phase looks more like the grind of deployment, customer discovery and real data collection. Corollary two: data holders have far more power than they realise (Ukraine is one example), and the asymmetry between ‘companies that can build frontier models’ and ‘entities holding proprietary deployment data from real economic activity’ may flip. Corollary three: labs may conquer vertical industries one at a time, and the winning move is to become the deployer yourself.

item.title: AI Makes Venture's Power Law Steeper, Not Gentler
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-a16z-ai-让风投的幂律变得更极端-而不是更温和/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-a16z-ai-让风投的幂律变得更极端-而不是更温和/
item.description: Of 3,000 venture firms, only 20 delivered 3x net returns for twenty straight years. For the first time, AI lets money convert directly into compute, and compute directly into product advantage — so the power law gets steeper, not flatter.
item.content:encoded:
Of 3,000 venture firms, only 20 delivered 3x net returns for twenty straight years. For the first time, AI lets money convert directly into compute, and compute directly into product advantage — so the power law gets steeper, not flatter.

Three frontline LPs/GPs lay out the allocation logic of venture in the AI era: why money can compound directly into advantage for the first time, and why LP and GP incentives point in exactly opposite directions. High information density, but the back half is worth more than the opening.

2:04 For the first time, money converts directly into product advantage
David George says the classic way to kill a startup used to be giving it too much money: it hires a thousand people, creating coordination problems, expense problems and warring priorities. This time is different — you can throw money straight into compute, and compute makes the product and the business better. This is a new form of increasing returns to scale in the AI era: the old mechanisms of brand, reputation and accumulated resources still operate, but capital itself has become a self-reinforcing factor of production for the first time. So a more extreme power law doesn't surprise him.

4:04 AI hit in four years what SaaS took fifteen to reach
Ram's comparison: AI has already reached $100 billion in revenue; SaaS took 15 years to reach the same point, AI took only 4, and demand penetration is nowhere near its ceiling. He argues the root of ‘you can pour money into these companies’ is that there is no upper bound on inference demand. More critically, AI is attacking every face of GDP at once — transportation, labor, services, capital, coordination — and no technology paradigm has ever hit so many parts of a $30 trillion GDP simultaneously. So for allocators this shouldn't be a satellite position; it should be core, or even super-core.

6:07 AI's TAM isn't software, it's the tasks being performed
Take healthcare: healthcare IT spends only $60 to $100 billion a year, but AI is attacking the value of actual labor and tasks — claims, billing, administration — which is a trillion-dollar industry. So AI's TAM can be more than 10x larger than traditional SaaS or healthcare IT. Ram says he ‘misjudged for a long time how big these outcomes could be’, and David admits the same. Another number: the US economy spends roughly 40x more on labor than on software. But David stresses this doesn't mean labor disappears — it means labor gets reinvented.

11:14 Of 3,000 venture firms, only 20 consistently hit 3x
Ram's team looked at data on 3,000 US venture firms: over the past twenty years only 20 consistently delivered 3x net returns, under 1%. And you don't need seven or eight funds over twenty years to clear the bar — three to four funds at 3x net TPPI is enough. What those 20 share: they got the category-defining company in every vintage. The comparison point is Cambridge's data — over the past decade venture's average net return was only 1 to 2x, worse than private equity, worse than public markets, and your money is locked up for ten years. So ‘did you get into one of those 20’ decides almost everything.

13:18 Mid-tier funds are being squeezed to death from both ends
Ram and David repeatedly invoke the ‘death of the middle’. Two ends survive: one is the very early, deeply vertical specialist fund, which moves fast and can grab the share that big funds also want; the other is the platform mega-fund that covers the whole lifecycle from seed to IPO. The funds in the middle — not early enough, not full-stack enough — are the hardest to compete from. David cites Endowment Eddie: interest in big funds is founder-driven, not LP-driven — founders want the brand that de-risks outcomes, scales, and brings customers and hires; LPs just follow along slowly.

21:43 AI makes it harder to tell what real traction is
Ram says AI makes their job harder than ever: rounds are bigger and faster, and traction in the industry has become confusing. A company comes out of an accelerator, hits $5 million ARR in a month, has no renewal cycle yet, and raises at a huge multiple — and these companies may be ‘singing’ to each other within the same cohort, or it isn't even ARR but some month multiplied by 12. Only one in nine such companies is genuinely special. So judging real traction can't rely on financial analysis; it requires understanding customers and talking to them directly. He cites Harvey: commercially strong early, but actual usage wasn't high, until reasoning models arrived and usage and engagement flipped completely.

26:56 GP and LP incentives point in exactly opposite directions
Ram says a GP gets fired for missing the next Facebook, the next Uber — that's an error of omission, and it's fireable. But an LP only gets fired for making a bad investment; not investing costs them nothing. So if you missed the frontier models but are roughly at benchmark, or even slightly below, your job is safe. For many LPs the upside itself isn't that attractive, so the ‘you'll miss the next generation’ pitch doesn't land with them. Ram thinks what LPs should actually do comes down to three things: access, selection, sizing. If only 20 of 3,000 firms do well, you should concentrate in those 15 to 20. When he sees someone allocated across 50, 60, 70 venture funds, he finds it hard to believe that portfolio beats the average.

38:20 Bolting AI onto a company doesn't make it Amazon
Ram punctures AI-era private equity in one line: putting Sears on a website doesn't make it Amazon — you have to build Amazon's logistics from scratch. He gives the counterexample: a company's first move is AI customer service, because it's the easiest fruit to pick, but without rebuilding around the workflow, customers used to dealing with humans churn fast, and every point of NPS decline ties directly to revenue decline, which stacked on debt spirals downward. Intercom is the positive case: bring the founder back, rebuild the entire business, build AI-native products, then sell — that's close to a ‘suicidal’ overhaul of the existing business, and extremely hard to pull off in private equity.

item.title: Opening Accounts for AI Agents: Credit Card Fees Can't Carry the Machine Economy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
item.description: Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.
item.content:encoded:
Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.

The part about how Coinbase uses AI internally is the most valuable: one "brain" per service, corrections must be written back, and the mechanism is concrete enough to copy; agent payments come with hard numbers, while the new drug section is more opinion than detail.

6:47 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents
Armstrong says agents are already generating a large volume of transactions worth a few cents: VC firms scraping paywalled data for research, recruiters crawling LinkedIn, one agent calling another specialized agent as a tool to fetch source data. But the minimum per-transaction fee on a debit or credit card is a flat 30 cents plus a percentage, so the old rails basically don't work below $1 — paying 30 cents to move 1 cent makes no sense. The number he gives: about 76% of the agentic commerce transactions they see are under 30 cents. This is the hardest reason stablecoins and crypto rails cut into the machine economy.

11:42 Build a "brain" for every service
Coinbase built a "brain" for every team, every repo, every service, and even every employee: it contains all the incidents that service has had, the financial controls that must be enforced, every A/B test that has been run, the complete GitHub history, and which PRs were accepted or rejected. When an agent comes to change code, it reads this brain first. The truly critical step: when a human reviewer finds the agent missed something, they are not allowed to just hand-edit and merge — that correction must be written back into the brain. That way one correction covers all future scenarios, and the one-shot PR rate keeps rising, which Armstrong calls "recursive self-improvement."

15:00 The CEO runs 10 agents changing code at once
Armstrong says now when he hits an idea or a bug, he no longer pings the team all day; instead he drops the comment into an internal harness (they call it Toshi) and sends a finished PR for review — he says it's addictive. He himself has the CEO writing features again: have an expensive frontier model break a complex feature into three phases, ten things per phase, then have it recommend which cheaper model to use for each subtask, then run 10 agents in parallel on phase one. He says during the time it took to record this podcast, all 10 things were done and waiting for his review.

17:02 What gets eliminated is tasks, not people
On whether AI will make companies smaller, Armstrong's judgment is: productivity is indeed rising, but that's a separate matter — what gets automated or eliminated is tasks, not people. He doesn't think a company like Coinbase will shrink to 10 people; rather, the people it has can do vastly more and everything speeds up; at the same time, two-person and five-person companies will indeed produce volumes that were previously unimaginable. The result is that the cost curve of revenue relative to headcount changes: the same group of people can produce much more, and long term margins should rise. He doesn't overstate it — some companies will still hire at the same pace.

18:33 88% of revenue no longer comes from Bitcoin trading
Armstrong cites numbers from the earnings report: 88% of revenue now comes from non-Bitcoin trading. Interestingly, Coinbase's stock price is still highly correlated with Bitcoin's price. He says he loves Bitcoin, considers it digital gold and sound money for everyone in the world, but crypto is updating every part of the financial system. The tokenized equity product he just announced is currently only available outside the US, and they are talking with regulators about a US path; he stresses these are real stocks — backed 1:1 by real securities held in custody, not synthetics, derivatives, or debt instruments.

21:57 Prediction markets are more than sports betting
Armstrong says prediction markets are growing extremely fast in the Coinbase app: within a few months of launch they reached about $100 million in annualized revenue, with quarter-over-quarter growth over 100%. Sports is indeed a part of it, and he thinks that's a form of entertainment worth celebrating — but he thinks it's much bigger than that, and the societal implications haven't been fully understood. The example he gives is policy: to judge whether a policy should be implemented, you could first form a prediction market on "what will the unemployment rate be one, two, three years after implementation." Beyond that are big questions with no clear settlement date like "is there a God," which he calls an opinion market, with mechanics like buying a stock — you're just betting on whether it will get better or worse.

31:53 Restoring cells to their youthful function
New Limit takes the epigenetic reprogramming route: it doesn't change cell type (the Yamanaka lab approach does), it only restores the cell's youthful function. The platform first uses AI to search the vast combinatorial space of transcription factors for candidates, runs large-scale pooled screens, then functional experiments (mostly animal models), and finally human trials. The first batch targets three cell types: hepatocytes, vascular cells, and T cells of the immune system. The first Phase 1 trial targets alcoholic liver disease (ALD), where patients have almost no options besides a liver transplant and survival after diagnosis at 12 months is very low. Armstrong estimates this one drug alone could be worth $20 billion if it succeeds, but the goal is for a 40-year-old to have the liver, immune system, and blood vessels of a 20-year-old.

41:10 What America lacks isn't land, it's sandboxes
Armstrong's interest in special economic zones comes from a "meta-question": what is slowing down progress — in many places it's overregulation. He mentions Coinbase invested in Prospera in Honduras, and thinks they've had ups and downs with the local government but are close to resolving it. During the campaign there was discussion of an idea called "freedom cities": the federal government holds vast tracts of land, take 10 or 100 square miles, and on that land you don't have to go through the usual EPA process, you can build data centers, nuclear power plants, unlimited drone delivery without needing FAA approval item by item — first try what works in a safe, controlled sandbox, and if it succeeds, push it back to the whole country through the normal process. He says the problem now is that in many cases there is simply no sandbox to try, and if entrepreneurs can't iterate they can't solve the problem.

item.title: Take a Spending Test Before You Marry: Tightwads and Spendthrifts Attract Each Other, and Divorce More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.description: Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes attract each other, but after marriage they have more money conflicts and lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.
item.content:encoded:
Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes attract each other, but after marriage they have more money conflicts and lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.

Medium information density. The first half is spending-personality research; the second half — on prenups, wedding spending, and who holds decision power over family finances — is more valuable. Skim-friendly.

7:05 A tightwad isn't frugal — spending physically hurts
Scott Rick and coauthors proposed in 2008 a spending scale running from tightwad to spendthrift. The core isn't how much you spend but ‘anticipatory pain’ — the emotional reaction you feel at the moment of paying. Tightwads feel too much pain from spending and spend less than they ideally would; spendthrifts feel too little and spend more than they ideally would. The scale measures the gap between your ‘ideal self’ and your actual behavior, so a very rich person can be a tightwad and someone near bankruptcy can be a spendthrift. On the show, Ben retook the test and scored 11, just over the tightwad line; Dan scored 16, an unconflicted consumer.

22:15 Tightwads and spendthrifts are exactly who attract each other
Research shows tightwads are more likely to marry spendthrifts than another tightwad. The authors' explanation: people are poor at introspection about what will attract them in a real partner; when someone else displays the same flaw you have, it instead reminds you of that negative trait. Hence ‘fatal fiscal attractions’ — the other person lacks your spending vice, so at first they seem especially attractive. But the excitement is temporary. Afterward, tightwad-spendthrift couples have more frequent money conflicts and lower marital happiness; the bigger the gap between the two on the scale, the more pronounced the conflict, even controlling for household debt and savings.

28:17 Everyone already has a default prenup
In Ontario it's called a marriage contract; elsewhere, a prenup. The key premise: when you marry, you already have a default agreement under your jurisdiction's family law, so the first step is to find out what the default terms are, then decide whether to write your own. Not marrying can also have legal consequences — cohabiting, or having children without marrying, can still produce legal effects on separation. Why do so few use one? First, optimism bias: engaged couples can accurately estimate the national divorce rate but estimate their own divorce probability far lower, so any agreement they sign doesn't seriously consider the scenario it's meant to govern. Second, signaling cost: proposing a prenup is itself treated as a negative signal of ‘lack of commitment to the relationship,’ making the other party less willing to raise it.

40:23 The more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk
A 2021 Journal of Consumer Policy paper surveyed more than 3,000 married people and, after controlling for income, demographics, and relationship factors, found the opposite of intuition: the more a man spent on an engagement ring, the higher the divorce risk; the more a woman spent on the wedding, the higher the divorce risk. Wedding-related debt stress may be one mechanism. Couples with the lowest divorce rates spent less than $1,000 on their wedding. But the same study found two kinds of wedding spending that predicted longer marriages: more guests, and going on a honeymoon — neither related to price. Ben's wedding cost about $300, with only his sister, parents, and wife present; Dan's cost about $5,000 for 150 people, saving money with a free photographer, a friend's cake, and gifts.

46:29 The benefits of merging finances may come from thinking, not doing
A 2022 meta-analysis covering six studies and more than 38,000 people found that couples who fully merge finances have higher relationship satisfaction and are less likely to break up, and this holds across cultures. A 2023 Journal of Consumer Research study found joint accounts promote communal norms, shared goals, and good feelings about ‘managing money as a team.’ But more counterintuitive is a 2025 paper by Johan Yana Pet: directing people's attention to an existing joint account rather than their separate individual accounts produces similar effects — that is, thinking of finances as ‘ours’ rather than ‘yours and mine’ itself makes people talk about money more and more effectively, regardless of how accounts are actually set up. Another 2022 paper found that increases in jointly held wealth raise life satisfaction, while increases in individually held wealth have no significant effect.

53:32 Financial infidelity is a deeper problem than spending disagreements
Financial infidelity is defined as: engaging in a financial behavior you expect your partner would disapprove of, then hiding it. A recent paper found that when one partner is more prone to financial infidelity than the other, couples are more likely to drift toward separate financial goals rather than shared ones, and it predicts lower financial well-being and relationship satisfaction; this holds even after controlling for mismatches like tightwad/spendthrift. Joint accounts can increase transparency, but if someone is deliberately hiding things, even a joint account can be supplemented with a hidden one, and the problem escalates from finances to trust. Dan's judgment: if someone is committing financial infidelity, switching to a joint account either forces them to find another way or puts the problem on the table and leads to a split — which is already beyond the scope of financial planning.

57:36 In household asset allocation, the husband's preferences are systematically amplified
A 2026 Review of Financial Studies paper found that Australian households, at the household level, incorporate on average 60% of the husband's risk tolerance into asset allocation and only 40% of the wife's, which the authors call a 20-percentage-point bargaining-power gap; half comes from observable characteristics like income and employment, and the other half is attributed to a gender effect. The husband's average bargaining power is 69% in Germany and 61% in the US; the three countries are statistically indistinguishable, but all exceed 60%. A 2021 Journal of Finance paper found that US households where the husband has high financial literacy are more likely to participate in the stock market than households where the wife has equal financial literacy, which the authors say is best explained by gender identity norms rather than ability differences; the mechanism suggested by randomized experiments is that female identity suppresses a wife's willingness to voice ideas, while male identity makes a husband less responsive to his spouse's input.

1:00:41 Overtrading costs men nearly a percentage point a year
Barber and Odean's 2001 study of 35,000 brokerage accounts found men trade 45% more frequently than women, consistent with the prediction that overconfidence leads to harmful overtrading. Trading has costs: overtrading reduces men's net returns by 2.65 percentage points a year and women's by 1.72 percentage points. Both groups hurt themselves by trading too much; women just did less of it. Dan adds that among the client couples he works with, the primary contact is almost evenly split between men and women; but when the man is the primary contact, the conversation is more about the portfolio, and when the woman is, it's more about planning. He also observes that some male clients ask questions they ‘feel they should ask,’ more like performance, while female clients almost never do.

item.title: MLB Built Baseball Castles in the Dominican Republic, and Also Grew the Lenders
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-papertrail-mlb-在多米尼加建了棒球城堡-也养出了放贷人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-papertrail-mlb-在多米尼加建了棒球城堡-也养出了放贷人/
item.description: MLB spends as much as $400 million a year in the Dominican Republic, but there is no draft and teams may sign players privately before they turn 16 — spawning a shadow industry of high-interest loans to players' families, with David Ortiz alleged to be part of it.
item.content:encoded:
MLB spends as much as $400 million a year in the Dominican Republic, but there is no draft and teams may sign players privately before they turn 16 — spawning a shadow industry of high-interest loans to players' families, with David Ortiz alleged to be part of it.

Investigative reporting, high information density, with concrete mechanisms and numbers; worth listening for anyone interested in the sports industry, platform governance, or emerging-market arbitrage.

3:07 MLB built 30 baseball castles in the Dominican Republic
MLB has built a talent pipeline in the Dominican Republic: all 30 teams have physical facilities near Santo Domingo, and a 20-minute drive from the airport brings you to gleaming complexes bearing Yankees and Mariners logos, which the show calls ‘baseball castles.’ The system generates as much as $400 million a year locally, and roughly 10% of current MLB players come from this Caribbean island. The castles are where the most promising prospects live and train; for an ambitious Dominican boy, getting in is the whole goal.

9:25 You can't sign until 16, but you can agree at 14
MLB rules say teams cannot sign players under 16, but when Belfi was 14, his coach pulled him and his parents into a video call, and on the other end was a representative of the Arizona Diamondbacks saying they wanted Belfi to become part of their family. In the Dominican Republic this practice is called an ‘early agreement,’ and all 30 teams do it. One MLB scout told the reporter that if you don't do early agreements, you'll be eaten alive and won't sign a single player you want. The United States has a draft; the Dominican Republic does not, so teams can only compete by locking up prospects earlier and earlier.

15:43 80% of Dominican signing bonuses are tied to loans
Early agreements create an awkward time gap: Belfi's family knew $1.8 million was coming, but they wouldn't see a cent for two years. The reporter describes these families as being in a state of mental whiplash — ‘about to be rich, but not rich yet’ — and some people saw a business in that. One lawyer estimates that 80% of MLB signing bonuses paid to Dominican prospects come with loans attached. The reporter found lenders on WhatsApp openly advertising to families with early agreements. Caraballo's first loan to Belfi's family was $25,000 in cash in exchange for $180,000 in the future; the second was $70,000 at 7% monthly interest, roughly 84% annualised — an illegal rate in most US states, but nothing in Dominican law prohibits it.

22:08 On signing day they went to the bank, and Belfi left empty-handed
The signing bonus was paid in two instalments, the first $900,000. When Belfi and his family got to the bank, Caraballo and the coaches were all there waiting for their cut: the coaches ultimately took $720,000, and Caraballo took the $180,000 he claimed he was owed. On his first trip to the bank, Belfi got nothing. Asked whether he realised it would go this way, he said he was somewhat disappointed but had more or less expected it — he trusted that his parents needed that loan, and trusted even more that this man who treated him like a mentor wouldn't take advantage of him.

23:13 The second payment was talked into ‘a fund with Ortiz’
Four months later the second payment arrived. Caraballo picked them up in a parking lot and told Belfi's parents on the way: you're poor, you don't know how to manage money, I can put the rest into a fund together with David Ortiz that pays you a monthly dividend, so you won't have to manage it yourselves. In a private room, Belfi watched in silence as his parents signed away nearly the entire second instalment. Then the scene at the bank spun out of control: a family friend and former coach publicly called Caraballo a ladrone (thief) and chased him around the bank, while Caraballo shot back that the coach just wanted a cut for himself. In the chaos Belfi put $196,000 into his personal account, and Caraballo left with the rest of the money and his bodyguards — without leaving the family, whom he had driven there, a ride.

27:25 A company co-owned by Ortiz and Caraballo
The reporter obtained more than a dozen of Caraballo's contracts, signed by players' parents, with children as young as 10, handing Caraballo control over the child's finances and baseball career decisions. Almost everyone interviewed said Caraballo told them Ortiz was his business partner. The reporter found registration records in Florida for a company called Big Poppy Sports Group listing both men; what the company did is unclear, and it was dissolved about a year later. Around the same time, Ortiz and Caraballo signed a contract with the parents of a 13-year-old Dominican prospect, promising training, housing and meals in exchange for 35% of a future signing bonus, and barring the child from leaving the baseball academy while also securing his representation rights. The family later sued, claiming the two failed to perform and the child never signed; the case was dismissed on procedural grounds.

34:38 One voice memo from Ortiz killed the international draft
MLB has long wanted an international draft, so that players from the Dominican Republic, Venezuela and elsewhere would be picked in order like American players, with signing bonuses determined by draft position rather than private deals struck years in advance with the families of teenagers. In 2022, during contract negotiations between MLB and the players' union, the international draft was an issue close to being settled. But a retired player sent a voice memo to a group of Dominican players and coaches, claiming in his usual hyperbolic style that more than 40% of the Dominican population depends on baseball for a living and that a draft would destroy the income of future generations. That player was David Ortiz. The day after the voice memo went out, the league and the union reached a contract, and the international draft idea was abandoned.

36:41 Ortiz called the reporter himself, then hung up
Before the reporter had even contacted Ortiz, Ortiz heard about the reporting and called him unprompted, but would not allow recording. It began amicably; he admitted he had invested in Caraballo's business, to the tune of millions of dollars, but would not say how much or which business. He said he doesn't deal directly with players, and that if anyone says otherwise, he has no idea what they're talking about. When the reporter asked whether he opposed the international draft because he holds previously unreported stakes in the Dominican baseball industry and a draft would destroy that business model, the friendly atmosphere ended there, and he hung up quickly. In a statement sent through his lawyer, Ortiz said his opposition to the draft was not out of personal interest but based on what he believed a draft would do to Dominican baseball; he confirmed a close friendship with Caraballo and a business relationship involving lending to coaches, but said he never knew about the investment fund and never agreed to take part in Caraballo's other businesses.

item.title: Insects Are Disappearing, but Pesticides Aren't the Biggest Killer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.description: Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture — it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.
item.content:encoded:
Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture — it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.

Medium information density; the first half leans into dragonfly genitalia for shock value; but the parts on pesticide regulatory blind spots and the successful eradication of the giant hornet are worth hearing.

8:55 The 70% decline was challenged, but the data keeps piling up
A decade ago, a European study covering 30 years of data showed insect total mass in one place had fallen 70%. Jessica herself raised doubts at the time: you can't directly compare heavy beetles with light mosquitoes, maybe it's just a shift in composition. But since then scientists have sampled repeatedly around the world, north to south, from the roots to the tips of the insect evolutionary tree, and they keep seeing the same pattern — a rate of decline never seen before. She concedes some pest cockroaches and some bee species are doing better, but in the other column the insects in decline are "still astonishingly high, and increasing."

19:02 Pesticides aren't a farming problem, they're a your-backyard problem
The host assumed the answer would be agricultural chemicals, but Jessica turned the spotlight on ordinary people. Agricultural pesticide use is tightly regulated, with rules on how much and what kind, and farmers don't want to spend more than they have to. But "you and I" can go out tonight and buy any pesticide, spray it wherever we like, with no regulation at all. She mentions the host ordering a pesticide from the US that is banned in Australia, and her response is "wear gloves and a mask." She calls the overall picture what her colleague David Wagner calls "death by a thousand cuts" — drought, floods, fire, nitrogen deposition, land-use change, noise, light pollution, chemical pollution, invasive species — with no single cure.

22:24 Colony collapse was only ever the story of managed honeybees
The colony collapse disorder that caused panic a decade ago was really only about Apis mellifera, the European managed honeybee, not native North American species. They get trucked around the country in huge trailers, live under heavy stress, and on top of that come Varroa mites and neonicotinoid pesticide residues. Jessica's critique: worrying only about this one domesticated, managed bee is like not worrying about any mammal going extinct except the cow we like to eat. What's actually needed is bee health as a whole, which is also why pollinator gardens have become popular — plant native species for every pollinator in the environment.

24:13 America's biggest irrigated crop is lawn
NASA researchers estimated in 2005 that the US has more than 30 million acres of lawn, golf courses included, and by surface area lawn is the single largest irrigated crop in the country. Jessica's advice is concrete: shrink the lawn, keep the part you play on, stop mowing the edges, let it go wild; or just plant a pollinator garden. She did exactly that on the slope in front of her house and got "garden shamed" by neighbors on the community social media, because a pollinator garden needs native plants of different heights and bloom times, and it looks ugly for the first few years.

27:16 Spotted lanternfly honeydew invites mold
The spotted lanternfly is a Hemiptera, its mouthparts a suction pump plus a straw that stabs into plants to drink sap, and an all-liquid diet means its waste is basically sugar water, known as honeydew. This sticky honeydew rains down on the environment, and certain molds and fungi grow on it, potentially harming plants. They have more than 70 host plants, their preferred host being the equally invasive tree of heaven, but they'll also take maples, apples, and unfortunately grapes. As they spread west toward California's big grape-growing regions, that's the real worry.

30:28 The giant northern hornet was completely eradicated
The so-called murder hornet has been renamed the giant northern hornet, and Jessica finds the old name a bit stigmatizing. She calls this story a success case for human collaboration: a homeowner saw an unfamiliar insect in their tree and, instead of ignoring it, reported it; the specimen reached a colleague at the Smithsonian and was identified; the government put up money, people on the West Coast mobilized immediately, found the location and cleared it. A piece of wood from that tree is now on display at the Smithsonian, because it held a batch of individuals. In December 2024, the USDA announced the hornet had been eradicated.

33:46 Cockroach milk is secreted through modified spiracles
Most cockroaches lay egg cases called oothika, which look like little coffee beans, and when they hatch all the larvae take a breath at once and pop the "little box" open. But cockroaches like diploptera punctata are ovoviviparous, and the mother feeds the embryos a milk-like secretion. Insects aren't mammals and have no nipples, so they modified their spiracles to secrete this milk. Compositionally it's high in protein, not all that different from mammalian milk, and cloudy white in color. A few years ago European scientists tried to pitch it as the next superfood. The current problem: extracting the milk usually means sacrificing the mother.

37:36 Fear of bugs is learned from your mother
Jessica says fear of insects is learned, not innate. A colleague at Rutgers ran an experiment: put babies and tarantulas together, and the babies aren't afraid on their own; but if the mother or primary caregiver shows disgust, the baby shows disgust too. Same with snakes and other animals. She uses her own two kids as an example: her daughter didn't start daycare until nearly one and was never afraid of bugs; her son started daycare at six weeks, and the daycare teacher was afraid of bugs and would scream and try to swat them, so the son grew up afraid of bugs — even though his own mother isn't. Once this learned behavior forms, it's very hard to change.

item.title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.description: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
item.content:encoded:
Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.

Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; the value is in the concrete scenes and in how one play grew. Skip it if you want methodology and industry judgment.

7:15 Disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm
Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Hanya (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of the sisters had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at New Year, her feeling was that it was "like walking a little dog or cat." Later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. Once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another mother, who is visually impaired, was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, on the grounds that "you can't see, you can't raise a child"; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These testimonies made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

11:19 Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair, and when she moved she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs; the chairs were hung all over with things, cartload after cartload. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would have been done in half a day. The colleague was stunned for a moment and said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she did not have a single able-bodied friend, and even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people don't even have the chance to meet, "you have no chance of inclusion at all." That was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre.

14:19 Writing the able-bodied as the discriminated original sinners
Leyi Theatre's first play, Reverse Future (逆转未来), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification such as electronic eyes and cochlear implants; the remaining few able-bodied become original sinners because of "the crime of starting the nuclear war," marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic is that since she herself is a situs inversus person, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning all the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights the able-bodied have to fight for — what she calls writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The core of the plot: an original-sinner father, to spare his son from suffering for his able-bodied body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to saw off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about original sinners and augmented people.

22:25 How the unseen and the unheard partner up
Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in by deaf actor Li Ning during an audition to be his partner. His first reaction was blank: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace signs, tapping once when it was Wang's line. Director Ma Yan says there is already an international form of blind and deaf performers on stage together, the deaf person's hand on the visually impaired person's hand, so the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says deaf people had been around him since childhood, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with a communication barrier, for whom "communication was absolutely impossible," a barrier that was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign language interpretation, real-time captioning on a big screen, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

25:28 Visually impaired actors wear earphones and cheat on stage
Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact "cheating": they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and then delivered them on stage flawlessly, so the director had no way to assess them and could only wonder how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language, so he could only watch everyone signing while laughing along, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks became known.

30:36 She received the best play award from the ICU
In 2024 Reverse Future was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and was admitted to the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and a friend stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more food, thinking "how could it possibly be us." In the end they won Best Play, the festival's highest award, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood up and led the applause. The news reached the ICU at the same moment as the award, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. In October of the same year the play was invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, as the first disability-inclusive play and the only production in the "Nothing Is Impossible" section.

35:45 After writing this play, she changed her answer to not being born
The second play, I Choose to Be Born (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that parents must use brainwaves to inform the fetus of its health status and family environment once it reaches eight months, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families, there are deaf parents who must honestly tell their child you will be deaf too, a husband who deceives his wife into having a child, a family that favours boys over girls, and a final story adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script, because their life experiences were eerily similar, differing only in the type of condition. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had it to do over, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice.

36:45 The same question, and Cai Cong answers it the opposite way
The episode sets the deaf couple in I Choose to Be Born against the real Cai Cong (蔡聪): Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume that such a life was not worth starting merely because the child might also be visually impaired; they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument around this choice persists. The question the episode poses: when a family makes a choice, how much capacity to choose do they actually have.

item.title: Inheritance of acquired traits is proven in nematodes, not yet in humans
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.description: Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — change only the RNA in the brain and you change behavior three generations later.
item.content:encoded:
Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — change only the RNA in the brain and you change behavior three generations later.

35 minutes walks the whole conceptual chain from DNA to small RNAs, with the experimental designs and key numbers included; on the mammalian part the speaker repeatedly states what is unknown, so it won't hand you a conclusion you can apply.

4:37 The genome is the whole book, and each cell pulls out one page
Every cell carries the same genome. Rechavi's analogy is that every room holds an IKEA manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out just one page, and that page is RNA, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. The messenger RNA that actually encodes protein is only a small part of RNA: less than 2% of the genome's sequence encodes messenger RNA, while a great deal of the RNA that gets transcribed does other things, many of which remain unexplained. This distinction is the foundation for everything that follows — DNA determines which instructions can be opened, and only then does the question become whether lived experience can rewrite those instructions.

11:35 Two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits
Why, by default, can't what you learn in life be passed on? Rechavi attributes it to two barriers. The first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century August Weismann proposed what is now called the Weismann barrier — only germ cells can hand information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. The second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates all kinds of chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — roughly 90% in mammals and humans. The reason for erasing is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being limited to the few pieces one room happened to make.

12:46 It was opposed and desired, and not for reasons of data alone
This barrier theory kept acquired inheritance out of favor for a long time. Rechavi describes two sides: one is the theory, the barrier sitting right there; the other is the atmosphere the controversy itself creates. He gives Schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — Schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, and at the same time wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: nothing you do affects the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. Rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning. But he doesn't push that into ‘because everyone wants to believe it, it has promise’; he only says RNA is a new lead, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in the mammalian field.

16:20 A nematode can run hundreds of generations in one PhD
Why should you trust nematodes? The conditions Rechavi lists are concrete: a C. elegans is always 959 cells, 302 of them neurons, and since the 1980s it has had a complete connectome, like a subway map marking who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can watch neurons fire directly, and you can switch genes on and off with optogenetics; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, kept in a dish eating bacteria, in a highly controlled environment where nature and nurture can be separated; the generation time is 3 days, so one PhD can run hundreds of generations of nematodes. Under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in nematodes already has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it.

21:20 Offspring that can't make small RNAs still resist viruses
The experimental design is clean enough to read by color: use a fluorescent virus, and if the virus replicates successfully the nematode turns green, while if it is destroyed it stays black. First let nematodes be infected by the virus and destroy it, then knock out the machinery for making small RNAs in their offspring — these offspring have no ability to make small RNAs from scratch themselves. Then infect them with the same virus. If they still turn black, the only explanation is that they inherited small RNAs from their parents. That is exactly what happens: all the offspring are black, and the resistance can be passed on for several more generations. Sequencing can directly read those small RNAs matching the viral genome, and only the offspring of parents that had been infected have them. These nematodes have no T cells or B cells; they defend against viruses with RNA, and this mechanism is RNA interference, which won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

24:46 The brain and heredity don't speak the same language
The boldest question in this episode is: can the brain leave information for the next generation? Rechavi points out that the obstacle is translation — the brain stores information in the three-dimensional structure of synaptic connections, while any heritable information must squeeze through the bottleneck of a single cell, the fertilized egg. He also offers another possibility: learning something may just mean removing a particular odorant receptor, in which case one RNA controlling that receptor would be enough to pass it on; such phenomena have been reported in mammals, but he says they haven't been proven convincingly enough, because no one has explained how the information gets from the brain to the germ cells. His own route bypasses translation: in a 2019 Cell paper, changing only the production of naturally occurring small RNAs in the nematode brain changed the foraging behavior of offspring, affecting them all the way to three generations later, with the mechanism landing on the germline gene sage-2, and also requiring the protein that physically carries RNA.

28:17 Mammals lack an RNA amplifier
Why can nematodes do it while mammals must be doubted? The mechanism Rechavi gives is blunt: the nematode's secret is that it can keep amplifying these small RNAs, so the signal doesn't get diluted. In mammals there is no known comparable amplification mechanism, so the question becomes — how does a tiny bit of RNA affect the whole organism?
