One possibility is that it acts only very early in development: at that point there are only a few cells, and it might even act on the placenta formed during pregnancy, after which development is steered off course step by step and problems such as metabolism follow. This is the idea of the developmental origins of health and disease. He also frames RNA's role in mammals as a candidate rather than a conclusion: small RNAs are the leading candidate for transmitting protective or harmful effects of stress, but ‘in mammals we don't know, and time will tell’.

31:07 RNA is more plastic than DNA, so start with diagnostics
The applications come in three layers. The nearest is diagnostics: in Israel, most couples preparing to have children get DNA diagnostics for genetic diseases, but no one currently looks at RNA; if the mechanism were clearer, RNA would be another layer, a whole new world, and there may be certain RNAs associated with disease. The advantage is that it isn't fixed the way DNA is — DNA is yours, and if you can't change it you can only choose another embryo; RNA is plastic. Only a step further out is intervention: in rodent experiments, overfeeding causes problems in the next generation, but if the mice are made to exercise, this abnormal inheritance is corrected; when doing IVF, perhaps you could change the RNA composition of the things you introduce. Rechavi is restrained about the timeline: he says this doesn't happen now, it's science fiction, but if it were figured out, he has also imagined telling someone preparing for IVF, ‘you should go run on the treadmill for a while’, which would change your RNA profile.

item.title: Stolen Goods Sell for 70-80% of Retail, and Retail Theft Is Now an Industry
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.description: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the identifiers and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Networked goods fetch 70-80% of retail, while T-shirts and deodorant bring in only about a third.
item.content:encoded:
Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the identifiers and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Networked goods fetch 70-80% of retail, while T-shirts and deodorant bring in only about a third.

High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorized, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the state of federal legislation, with plenty of hard numbers.

8:19 A third of shrink is self-inflicted
Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious, which Scott describes as the things we do to ourselves versus the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The industry line that has circulated for years is that of malicious shrink, roughly 40% comes from internal employees, 35% from people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages move only within a few points each year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that they have been underreported ever since COVID, with neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting fully capturing it.

22:52 Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal, and these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out to exchange for money — so they will get physical, and they have. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and some have been killed. That's why asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene, just to back off. His attitude is that he is willing to trade shrink for human safety every single day, and management and the board will back that decision.

23:53 RFID dies the moment it enters a steel store
Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and yet in 2026 is still expensive and hard to scale. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains what's peculiar about Home Depot: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, essentially a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read and only actively transmitting solutions work. He also says tag costs are now almost zero, and the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits is extremely costly. They have tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but retrofitting an entire production line for a single drill is very hard to scale.

25:58 Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
The division of labor works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs to go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — which might be a garage, a warehouse or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store labels and electronic tags before reselling, and the money flows up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a small crew of just a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, large platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backward from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

35:19 Selling one combo kit requires 4.2 restocks
Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there is a combo kit priced at $799, and every time one sells, they have to restock 4.2 times. Take that to finance and they immediately understand it's a gross margin problem — as long as locking up breaks even or even makes a little money, it's justified. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and if they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up a carefully selected set of categories, with a QR code to summon an associate who unlocks it in an average of 90 seconds; and locking up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rise, because the goods are finally in stock.

39:23 A fake bill of lading can drive the goods right out
In the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion, where whole containers are rerouted at the port or transload warehouse and taken elsewhere, sometimes even loaded back onto a container ship and hauled away; second, a driver drives eight hours across state lines, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and moves boxes; third, forged bills of lading and pickup orders, made to look real with AI, where a driver pulls in, says he's picking up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new may not be the methods but the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the area that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years, with trains sitting in a yard getting cracked open by a crowd; and the other side has good intelligence, hitting not every car but only the one carrying guns or electronics.

41:28 AI in security is an efficiency tool
Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closing and handing over to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They have just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores, letting existing cameras run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to identify a particular combination of suspicious behaviors and then recognize the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

44:30 Seven years ago no one cared; now there's a federal bill
He says he is now very optimistic. INFORM is probably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it has bipartisan cosponsorship, it has passed the House, and it is attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, with the president also saying he will sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources, and the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination center. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: no one took it seriously, and the prevailing mood was still decriminalization and defunding the police.

item.title: Baseball's stadium music isn't accompaniment — it's how fans take the game back
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
item.description: Baseball's official historian thinks stadium music is too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns spectators into part of the game.
item.content:encoded:
Baseball's official historian thinks stadium music is too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns spectators into part of the game.

Medium information density: the first half is baseball music history, and only the second half, the Nancy Faust story, is really worth it. Worth listening for anyone into sports, live experience, or fan culture.

0:00 One walk-up song can turn a passerby into a fan
Host Randa Abdel Fattah says she was indifferent to baseball for most of her life, until Mets pitcher Edwin Diaz's walk-up song Narco in 2022 changed that. Diaz is a closer, usually entering at a key moment in the late innings, and the team uses his walk-up song to tell the opponent "the fun's over, this one's ours." The entrance video went viral, the team started handing out plastic trumpets to fans, mascots Mr. and Mrs. Met pretended to play trumpets, and eventually the team flew the original artist, Timmy Trumpet, in from Australia to perform live. The host says if you were in the stands then, the feeling was electric.

6:18 The official historian finds the ballpark too loud
MLB's official historian John Thorne says plainly that he doesn't like entrance music. What he misses is the quiet between half-innings — quiet that makes other sounds louder and clearer: the strange sound of a bat hitting a baseball, the same sound when Babe Ruth hit, and when Josh Gibson did; the dull thud of a leather glove catching a fly ball; a coach yelling at a player to keep running and steal second. He thinks nonstop audio, the endless fight for fans' attention, may have robbed a kid who goes to the ballpark to dream of that right.

10:31 Take Me Out was originally a women's suffrage song
The seventh inning stretch was originally literal: stand up, move your legs, get the blood flowing. It became a musical moment thanks to a 1908 song, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, which was actually about women's suffrage. The protagonist in the original lyrics is Katie Casey, a baseball fan who knows all the players' names, gets upset when the umpire makes a bad call, and knows what to do when the score is tight — she gets the whole crowd to sing along. From this a new genre, the "baseball song," was born, flooding sheet music, cylinder records and 78s in the 1910s.

12:35 The baseball song boom was publishers, not fans
John Thorne points out that the 1910s wave of baseball music was less about fans liking it than publishers liking it — it was essentially a marketing tool to pull people into the ballpark. The evidence is the number of copycats: George M. Cohan released Take Your Girl to the Ball Game almost the same week, followed by imitations like I Want to Go to the Ball Game. But despite Tin Pan Alley producing so many baseball songs, large-scale singalongs at actual ballparks remained rare, and John says the main reason was technical: sound systems were too primitive, and before radio took hold, a brass band was still the best accompaniment.

17:47 That 1977 singalong broke the opposing pitcher
On a muggy July night in Chicago in 1977, the White Sox were down two runs to the Kansas City Royals. After the White Sox put runners on first and second, people in the stands started singing Hey Hey Goodbye, louder and louder, until more than 45,000 fans joined in and the announcers had to raise their voices to be heard over the singing. The White Sox then erupted — bases loaded, bases cleared, four runs in — and the other side was forced to change pitchers. As the pitcher walked off the mound, Chicago fans "saw him off" even louder. Nancy Faust says she was thinking "did I hear that right," because this wasn't the kind of thing you normally heard at a ballpark — it was more like mockery.

23:51 She scored players with songs, and fans fed her ideas
In her first years with the White Sox, Nancy Faust still played a set repertoire: the national anthem, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, and the hour when the crowd came in. In her third year she started improvising, playing whatever she saw. When Dick Allen came up, the crowd would leave the restrooms and popcorn stands, so she played the then-popular Jesus Christ Superstar, and when he hit a home run the place went crazy. Fans sitting around her booth started offering her ideas: one player used to work at a watch counter, got stuck there when the store closed, so when he came up she played Does Anybody Really Know What Time It Is. She says she was "the soundtrack to whatever was happening," not just scoring the players.

25:52 An opposing pitcher admitted the singing shook his confidence
After that 1977 singalong, one opposing pitcher told reporters: you're standing on the mound, there are men on base, Zisk is in the batter's box, thirty thousand people are singing Kiss It Goodbye, and that shakes your confidence. Nancy Faust later read in a book that players recalling those years said they hated hearing that sound, and winced when they heard na-na-goodbye. And White Sox slugger Richie Zisk said of those same fans: I don't know if they came to see us or we came to see them, but I can tell you it fired us up. Nancy's conclusion: I guess I did have an impact, I just didn't know it at the time.

28:56 She can't read music, it's all by ear
Every song Nancy Faust improvised over her career, she did by ear — she can't read music. Hum a few bars of anything and within seconds she'd play it back on the organ. She retired from the White Sox organist job in 2010, White Sox fan and former President Barack Obama personally wrote to congratulate her on her career, and the booth she sat in for decades is now named after her. She still occasionally comes back for special occasions, like Pope Night, playing Gotta Have Faith and Don't Stop Believing.

item.title: Iron Age Ireland had no Celtic invasion, only trade and language
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-ancients-爱尔兰铁器时代没有凯尔特人入侵-只有贸易和语言/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-ancients-爱尔兰铁器时代没有凯尔特人入侵-只有贸易和语言/
item.description: The traditional story says Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.
item.content:encoded:
The traditional story says Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.

Medium information density, with a long setup in the first half. The real value is in the second half, on Celtic identity, sacral kingship and the Fianna warband, suited to listeners interested in pre-Roman Europe.

2:18 Why the Irish Iron Age is the murkiest period
John Waddell says the Irish Iron Age is the darkest stretch of Irish prehistory, partly because people at the time practised cremation. In much of Europe the dead were buried with quantities of fine grave goods, whereas cremation plus burial destroys a great deal of useful archaeological evidence. So despite very fine metalwork and monuments, the absence of burial evidence makes this history especially hard to read. He also points out that using the phrase "Celtic Iron Age" to describe the period amounts to sticking an ethnic label on an era, adding another layer of trouble to an already complicated story.

9:28 Sea routes connected people rather than isolating them
Waddell repeatedly stresses an underrated fact: in prehistory, waterways were channels connecting people, not barriers. Ireland and Britain are islands, and people habitually assume islands mean isolation, but coastal routes and river routes were very likely the main means of connection. Before the Romans laid straight roads, travel by water was far easier than travel by land. This means we have consistently underestimated how connected the populations of prehistoric Britain and Ireland were. The Irish Sea was itself a connecting force, and the English Channel linked England to the continent.

10:31 Sacred sites sat on high ground, not by rivers
Tristan asks whether Iron Age settlements were all close to rivers and coasts. Waddell's answer is unexpected: famous sites like Tara, Rathcroghan and Navan Fort are not obviously on major routes. Each sits on high ground in its own different way, and these locations may have carried a kind of sanctity since the Neolithic. Tara was already an important burial place before 3000 BC, and its story runs into the medieval period, representing more than 4000 years of ritual activity. The importance of these places comes from accumulated time and religious meaning, not from rivers and sea routes.

15:38 A sacral king who fails or is wounded is deposed
Waddell draws a key concept out of medieval Irish texts: sacral kingship. The king of Tara was not a political strongman; his fundamental duty was to maintain cosmic order. If a sacral king could not bring good harvests, he was deposed. Another feature was that his body had to be flawless: once a sacral king was wounded, scarred or deformed, he was deposed. Waddell thinks this ritual may eventually be traceable in the archaeology of Britain and Ireland, indicating that in the Celtic era, the pre-Roman period, certain tribal rulers did carry a sacred quality.

21:43 The Celts were not invaders but a language community
The traditional story is that around 500 BC, Celtic-speaking peoples brought knowledge of iron to Ireland. Waddell says this is wrong. His best definition of the ancient Celts is "people who spoke Celtic", not an ethnic or racial definition. Ireland in the pre-Roman period was undoubtedly Celtic-speaking, but archaeology finds almost no evidence of immigrants in the Iron Age or the Late Bronze Age. Instead, from around 1000 BC there is abundant archaeological evidence of trade and exchange between Britain and Ireland, with the Thames, the Rhine, the Rhône, the Saône, the Loire and the Danube all serving as major corridors. Trade and exchange means movement of people, and people carried myths, legends and language with them. The Celtic languages most likely took shape gradually amid this Late Bronze Age surge of connectivity.

31:04 The Banquet Hall is really a ceremonial processional way
On the hill of Tara there is a monument called the "Banquet Hall", a pair of very long parallel earthworks. Waddell's colleague Conor Newman established that it was never a banquet hall — it is far too large to be any kind of hall. Standing between the banks, you find you cannot see the world outside, because the banks are still high even in their ruined state. Newman proposed that it was a processional way running from the northern end of the hill to the centre of the summit, used for royal inauguration rituals. There are gaps in the banks that let the procession look left and right at the burials and other monuments on either side, reminding the person about to become sacral king of the stories of ancestors and predecessors. Waddell compares it to Rome's Appian Way, lined on both sides with tombs.

33:07 Beneath Tara lies a timber circle bigger than Stonehenge
Geophysical survey on the hill of Tara revealed a huge circular timber structure, four to five times the scale of Stonehenge. It was built around 2000 BC and at the time would have stood on the hilltop as prominently as Stonehenge, but today there is no trace of it on the ground — only aerial photographs show the faint outline of the circle. Waddell says this reminds us that large timber circles earlier than Stonehenge are a feature of the prehistoric landscape of Britain and Ireland. Tara's burials have another detail: many of them intersect one another, as if new graves were deliberately laid partly over old ones to connect with ancestral remains, both legitimising one's own existence and conveying some kind of story.

39:22 The forgotten king Dathi and a Swiss myth
Waddell tells the story of an almost forgotten king, Dathi, associated with Rathcroghan in western Ireland. In medieval legend, Dathi was the last pagan king of Ireland, said to have campaigned on the European continent, possibly reaching the foot of the Swiss Alps, and to have been struck dead by lightning at the foot of the Alps, with his body carried back to Ireland and buried at Rathcroghan. The story was especially popular in the 19th century, because some people took it as proof that Irish military power reached far overseas. But Waddell says it looks like pure fabrication: there was never any Irish invasion of Switzerland. Dathi most likely only raided Britain occasionally. He was later overshadowed by the more famous warrior Cú Chulainn and gradually forgotten.

item.title: What Solo Founders Lack Isn't Hands, It's Someone to Make Them Tell the Truth
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-solofounders-单人创始人最缺的不是人手-是有人逼你说真话/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-solofounders-单人创始人最缺的不是人手-是有人逼你说真话/
item.description: Julian's diagnosis of five solo founders points at almost the same thing every time: without a co-founder, you lose the person who forces you to face what you actually did today.
item.content:encoded:
Julian's diagnosis of five solo founders points at almost the same thing every time: without a co-founder, you lose the person who forces you to face what you actually did today.

Five founders each bring one real problem, and Julian's live diagnosis is more concrete than any course. But this is public office hours — there's no deep case teardown.

3:04 A few hundred paying users means you haven't given them something worth paying for
Utkar's Game Native has 1.25 million users, but only a few hundred pay $5 to $10 a month for a Discord role, priority support and early access. Julian's read is blunt: all of that is "bonus," not core value — it's essentially a Patreon-style fan club, where people pay to support you, not because it's genuinely a good deal. His standard: a few hundred paying out of 1.25 million is precisely the proof that you haven't yet offered something truly worth paying for. And don't charge by taking away features people already have — create something new in the future that users haven't tried yet.

11:08 A solo founder has no accountability partner, and that's the deadliest part
Julian says solo founding is hardest from zero to one because "there's no accountability partner." He uses the gym as an analogy: if you've already agreed to train with someone every day, you're more likely to actually show up. Early on, with no customers, everything is fuzzy, and you're the only one judging whether you're spending your time right. His antidote: be a little kinder to yourself, while staying honest about what you're actually doing each day. He also names a default trap — writing code is "the addictive default option," because it always makes you feel like you're making progress, but the only thing that truly settles the question is paying customers.

18:13 Let the lab see its own gap first, then sell the solution
Ryan sells RL environments and benchmarks to frontier labs. Julian endorses his path: rather than leading with generic data, first use a public benchmark to get the lab to admit "we really do have this gap," and then offer that you can fill it. Ryan says this is already standard practice among frontier-lab data vendors — show that some model fails at some capability, and a few months later the research lead comes to you asking whether they can train on your data. Ryan's benchmark is a bunch of frontier models playing Werewolf against each other; what it measures isn't who wins, but reasoning ability, who lies best, and who lies most.

21:16 You don't need to be the best, you need to be the only
Ryan worries that being solo will make labs not take him seriously. Julian says the worry is partly valid, but only if you're competing head-on with others. He quotes Kevin Kelly: you don't want to be the best, you want to be the only. So the question isn't "how does this team look," it's "is this the only person who can help us solve this problem." He also says the solo thing is "more in your head than in anyone else's" — you can absolutely answer: I'm just starting out, I only work with a few people, I'll be hiring, and I have AI leverage.

26:20 Users don't want features, they want a button they can press
Charlie is torn between building the workflow features customers ask for and going straight at the AI brain that would eliminate all workflows. Julian tells the Magic School story: founder Adil was a former high school principal who wanted teachers to use ChatGPT, ran a whole-school training, and nobody actually used it. He judged that the blocker wasn't AI being too weak, but that a blank chat box is too scary — it can do anything, and therefore feels like it can do nothing. So Adil built dozens of "micro-apps," each doing one specific thing. 100 users the first week, 1,000 the second. Julian's conclusion: the feature requests users make are actually them telling you the jobs to be done.

31:24 A slow deal may not be an efficiency problem, it may be an incentive problem
Charlie says both sides of a wholesale trade know exactly what they want, yet it takes two or three weeks of back-and-forth emails and CSVs to close. Julian doesn't answer directly; instead he asks a counterintuitive question: if everyone wants to compress the time, why hasn't the time been compressed? Could some incentive be deliberately stretching it out? He says sometimes things drag on for a reason — just not the reason everyone assumes. He also suggests using frequency × severity to decide which problem to tackle first.

39:28 Build the brain first, don't start with the body
Andy wants to build "describe a robot, get a design and a 3D-printed kit," and is torn about whether to bring someone in to split software and hardware. Julian asks back: if you were given a full-time person and enough money, what would you do differently? Andy says he'd put it all into 3D printing and hardware testing. So Julian suggests: could you skip hardware for now, run the character on a phone, put it on the desk as a base — the character can't move, but it exists; then the robot's first boot is releasing the character from the phone into the physical world. He uses dementia as an analogy: what makes a person a person isn't an exoskeleton, it's memory, a way of communicating, the look in their eyes when they recognise you. So early on, the body may matter less than the mind.

43:35 Different characters move differently, and that's exactly the hardware problem
Andy explains why he can't let go of physicality: Pikachu, Snoopy, a rover — they move through physical space in completely different ways. If you want to bring Pikachu or an owl into the real world as a robot, you have to find a solution for "different characters moving in different ways." That's why he weights physicality so heavily. Julian concedes the point holds, and says if he built the owl it would be "a real hoot." This is the only moment in the session where a founder pushes back on Julian's advice head-on.

item.title: Ashurbanipal's Library: He Was Both a Tyrant and the Earliest Book Collector
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-stuffmissed-亚述巴尼拔的图书馆-他既是暴君-也是最早的藏书家/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-stuffmissed-亚述巴尼拔的图书馆-他既是暴君-也是最早的藏书家/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Ashurbanipal locked defeated kings in dog kennels and forced people to make bricks from their ancestors' bones — and he also built humanity's earliest systematic library, keeping the Epic of Gilgamesh alive to this day.
item.content:encoded:
Ashurbanipal locked defeated kings in dog kennels and forced people to make bricks from their ancestors' bones — and he also built humanity's earliest systematic library, keeping the Epic of Gilgamesh alive to this day.

Medium information density; the first half is Mesopotamian background, and the second half — how the library was preserved and deciphered — is where the real value is.

0:01 The same man, two completely opposite first impressions
At the British Museum, Tracy read the exhibit panels on Ashurbanipal's library and thought, "this guy's library is astonishing"; in the same gallery Patrick read the other set of panels about him as king of Assyria, and came away thinking, "this guy was really cruel." The same material can support two entirely opposite impressions at once, and the rest of the episode picks apart that contradiction: he did put a conquered Elamite king on his chariot and lock a rival in a dog kennel, and he also ordered texts from across the empire copied and sent to the capital.

4:04 You cannot lay out a timeline for Mesopotamia at all
Tracy wanted to open the episode with a basic timeline and found she couldn't. Mesopotamia spans more than three thousand years from the first cities, with civilizations, kingdoms and empires overlapping and influencing one another, so a linear timeline is itself a distortion. Assyrian history is divided into Early Assyrian (from about 2600 BCE), Old Assyrian (from about 2025 BCE), Middle Assyrian (from about 1363 BCE), and Neo-Assyrian (911 to 609 BCE), followed by a post-empire period. Assyrian people still exist today: roughly three to five million people in Iran, Iraq, Syria and Turkey identify as Assyrian.

9:10 The father split the empire in two to prevent civil war
Esarhaddon's father Sennacherib had Babylon utterly destroyed and even diverted canals to flood the ruins, and was later assassinated by his own sons, which was read as divine punishment for destroying Babylon. Esarhaddon rebuilt Babylon and positioned himself as its "governor" rather than its king. In 672 BCE he divided his two sons' roles: Shamashumukin took Babylon, and Ashurbanipal was made crown prince of Assyria. The arrangement was meant to prevent a repeat of the civil war that had attended his own accession. The episode says explicitly that this will come back later — because the brothers eventually turned on each other.

9:10 He got an education a king was not supposed to have
By the time Ashurbanipal was made crown prince, his education had already begun. He learned horsemanship, chariot driving, archery, military tactics and court etiquette — the standard royal package. But he also studied literature and history, knew multiple Sumerian and Akkadian dialects, and could read and write cuneiform. The episode stresses that kings of this era were not usually educated this academically, and often were not literate at all — literacy was the business of scholars and scribes. The likely reason he got this education is that early in life he was not being groomed entirely as the heir.

13:14 In the reliefs, he wears writing tools on his belt
Ashurbanipal was a patron of the arts, building temples and palaces and commissioning vast numbers of reliefs. Many depict him fighting, lion hunting, and going about daily life amid wealth and luxury; some show the severed heads of enemies. The episode singles out one detail: in many depictions he wears a riding stylus on his belt, including in scenes where he is killing lions with a sword — Holly jokes that he may have wanted to write in his diary after killing a lion. The reliefs from his reign are regarded as the peak of Assyrian art, and the lion-hunt reliefs are now in the British Museum.

15:19 Cruelty was not his invention; he took it to an extreme
The episode draws a clear distinction: practices like displaying enemies' severed heads were normal among rulers of ancient Mesopotamia; but in the depictions he commissioned and in records others left, Ashurbanipal is seen as having pushed this to an extreme. Specific examples include: salting the land after putting down a revolt, forcing people to grind up their ancestors' bones to make bricks for a palace, making the defeated Elamite king pull his chariot in a triumphal procession, and forcing one rival to live in a dog kennel. About that rival, some accounts say he was forced to wear a dog collar, others that a chain was run through his jaw.

21:39 This was the earliest systematically collected library
The library was built in the capital, Nineveh, and tablets have been found in the Southwest Palace, the North Palace, and around the temples of Ishtar and Nabu. The episode stresses two things: first, it is unclear whether these were the library's original storage locations or the result of tablets scattering after the city's destruction; second, this is one of the earliest known libraries to be systematically acquired and organized — a deliberately collected, curated body of knowledge, and the largest collection of Assyrian texts in the world. Excavations yielded more than twenty thousand tablets and fragments, many with standardized colophons, indicating a systematic method of labeling and cataloguing. The total number of complete tablets is actually unknown.

22:39 He ordered the whole empire to hand over books, and knew who to ask
Ashurbanipal ordered temples and palaces across the empire to send texts to Nineveh, usually by having a copy made, with him receiving the copy or the original. Surviving documents show he actually wanted the originals, and that subordinates may have "creatively misinterpreted" the instructions in order to keep originals in their own temples or collections. Surviving correspondence also shows he knew exactly where to look for texts he wanted, and who might hold works he did not know about but that were worth acquiring. Holly describes him as having a network of scholarly acquisition librarians. Some texts in the library were written by him, and many tablets carry colophons he wrote.

item.title: No Irreplaceable Leaders, Only Irreplaceable Luck
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-tyler-没有不可替代的领袖-只有不可替代的运气/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-tyler-没有不可替代的领袖-只有不可替代的运气/
item.description: Diamond says history has no irreplaceable leaders — Genghis Khan just happened to be born on the wettest grassland in two thousand years. But people like Rachel Carson and Resnick really did move things forward by ten or twenty years.
item.content:encoded:
Diamond says history has no irreplaceable leaders — Genghis Khan just happened to be born on the wettest grassland in two thousand years. But people like Rachel Carson and Resnick really did move things forward by ten or twenty years.

Diamond is 89, talking about leaders, geographic determinism, Papua New Guinea and Bach cantatas. Medium information density, but the second half — on environmental optimism and writing method — is where the value is.

1:09 No irreplaceable leaders, only irreplaceable timing
Diamond's answer to ‘who is the most irreplaceable leader in human history’ is ‘no one.’ The reason is not that leaders don't matter, but that time washes out the difference: Jesus was a charismatic founder, but the Roman Empire of the same period had half a dozen other prophets; Genghis Khan built the largest land empire from China to Poland, but recent research found that the wettest period on the steppe in the past two thousand years happened to fall right around his birth — had he been born twenty years earlier, two hundred miles farther away, we would never have known his name. From this Diamond distinguishes two kinds of questions: why you and I speak English right now, the answer lies in the domesticable plants and animals of the Fertile Crescent, nothing to do with individuals; why Amazon is what it is today, the answer is Bezos alone.

13:50 Rachel Carson moved environmentalism forward by ten years
Cowen challenges Diamond with the environmental Kuznets curve: once per capita income reaches 28,000, countries turn green on their own — is Carson replaceable? Diamond concedes the movement would have come anyway, but stresses she at least moved it forward by about ten years — the day after her “Silent Spring” was published, a senator announced a government investigation into toxic chemicals. More crucial was her position at the time: in that era a professional scientist writing popular science was seen as ‘selling out,’ and she was not a university professor, so no one could say that of her; she was a woman, wrote like a poet, would read her drafts aloud to hear them. Diamond says that even today's best science writer, Richard Dawkins, doesn't write as well as she did.

18:00 The pomegranate juice industry waited five thousand years to appear
Cowen tests Diamond's replaceability theory with the pomegranate juice industry: without the Resnick family, America would eventually have gone down this road anyway. Diamond says no. Pomegranates were domesticated five or six thousand years ago, but there was never a global pomegranate juice industry, because pomegranate juice is extremely hard to make — you cut an orange and squeeze, but the pomegranate's value is inside an extremely hard rind, and the contents are not pulp but small seeds; scaled production requires a three-story-tall tower that crushes whole pomegranates rind and all. In 2002 America had 22 pomegranate growers, 21 of them small farmers with no money and no motive. Lynda Resnick put in about two hundred million dollars and waited 18 years before starting to make money. Companies like Coca-Cola and Nestlé would never allow a division to invest 150 million dollars and not be profitable for 18 years.

29:32 Face-to-face social skills are collapsing off a cliff
Diamond's advice to a 25-year-old who wants to become influential: learn to talk to people face to face, put down indirect communication tools. He did 60 years of fieldwork in Papua New Guinea, and saw Chevron bring in international lawyers from Switzerland to negotiate with villagers who had never left their village — the lawyers thought they'd close it in a day, but the agreement reached on day one, on day two the villagers said ‘we've forgotten that agreement, the people who signed it don't count, these are a few other negotiators.’ The villagers had negotiated face to face their whole lives, with far more skill than the international lawyers. Diamond says that over the past 40 to 50 years he has watched social skills degrade, and in his 39-year-old child's generation it is especially striking, because most communication is no longer face to face, and people no longer understand each other.

33:54 New Guineans may be smarter than Westerners
Diamond answers ‘yes’ outright, and says some people hate him for it. His argument is that natural selection pushed in different directions: over the past ten thousand years European survival depended mainly on surviving smallpox, tuberculosis, measles and other infectious diseases, little to do with intelligence; the main causes of death in New Guinea were coping with an extremely difficult environment and coping with other New Guineans — warfare there was constant. So his impression is that New Guineans on average ask more questions and are smarter. He adds that Westerners usually think they're stupid because they use stone tools — but they lack metal tools because agricultural output was much lower, not because of intelligence. Cowen presses him on a Nature paper claiming West Eurasians have gotten smarter since the Stone Age; Diamond says he hasn't seen it, but for more than a century eugenicists have been trying to prove Europeans are smarter, with no evidence whatsoever.

39:24 The Industrial Revolution happened in Britain because it is an island
Diamond rejects Greg Clark's hypothesis that the British became more patient by lowering their time preference through intermarriage. His explanation is geography: Britain is an island, needs no standing army, and is not constantly invaded — the last successful invasion was 1066. Not needing an army, it gradually developed democracy, and democracy is a productive form of government. Britain also sits on the Atlantic coast, and like the Netherlands, Spain and Portugal, is one of the countries that could spread across the world, because the Atlantic coast was the testing ground for seafaring technology. He mentions that in the 1600s Britain cut off its king's head, and Parliament became powerful. On Daron Acemoglu and Jim Robinson's extractive vs inclusive institutions theory, Diamond says he has learned more from Jim Robinson than from any individual in the past 20 years, but thinks they give geography less weight than he does.

44:32 Big business and young people have made him cautiously optimistic
Diamond says that 20 years ago he would have said the most evil and destructive force in the world was big business, when big business basically didn't care about the environment. But over the past 20 years, big business has come to care more and more: Walmart leads on sustainable products, Unilever leads on sustainable fisheries, even oil companies. In 1999 the World Wildlife Fund sent him to Chevron's oil field in Papua New Guinea to do an environmental study; he expected it to be terrible, but found Chevron extremely cautious, because they knew that if they screwed up, New Guineans would sue them, and they wouldn't get the Norwegian oil field development contract either. Another source of optimism is young people: 25 years ago young people didn't care about the environment, now they care very much. The probability he gives is 51% good outcome, 49% bad outcome.

47:46 The most important question is not to find the most important question
Cowen asks what the biggest environmental problem is at the global macro level, and Diamond laughs and says this is why interviewing Diamond is frustrating: his answer is always ‘the most important thing is not to go looking for that one most important thing, because the world is complicated.’ He uses marriage as an analogy: a couple about to marry asks what the single most important thing for a happy marriage is, and the answer is not to go looking for that one most important thing — you need to get 37 things right, and if you get 36 right but are incompatible on sex or religion, the marriage breaks. Back to the question itself, he says there are three things we must get right: climate change, inequality, and nuclear risk — including the risk of nuclear war and nuclear winter.
